subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATIVE PROGRAMME FOR THE' SESSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATIVE PROGRAMME FOR THE' SESSION
speechtext:
On February 17, the day on which
we met, in reply to a question of mine the Prime Minister promised to indicate to the house in the course of a day or two the measures which were likely to come up at this session. So far as I have been able to-observe the Prime Minister has not done this. I should like to ask him if he would take an early opportunity to set forth in some detail' the proposed legislative programme for this session. This information is not important to myself, but I am sure it would prove helpful to a lot of the members in making future plans.
Right- Hon. IV. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): I shall be only too pleased to give my hon. friend the information he has asked for at as early a moment as it may be possible to give it with a completeness likely to be of help to hon. members. The leason I have not replied up to the present is that I did indicate at the time the question was first asked that I anticipated that the measures to be introduced this session would be confined almost exclusively to financial measures having to do with the war, the War Appropriation Act, the budget and supply.. Outside of these I do not know of any other measures of importance likely to be proceeded' with beyond those already appearing on the order paper.
It is possible that there may be some legislation with respect to the St. Lawrence waterway project, but up to the present time no agreement has been finally reached. Therefore, I am not in position to say when that particular measure will come before the house-Perhaps this will answer my hon. friend's question immediately, parliament has before it at the moment, so far as I am in a position to know, with the exception mentioned, the legislation of importance for this session.

Business of Parliament
On the orders of the day:

I note that His Majesty the King has proclaimed March 23 as a day of prayer for victory and peace. Will the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) indicate whether a similar proclamation is to be made in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On a previous occasion when I saw that His Majesty the King had made a proclamation for a day of prayer in the United Kingdom, I thought it would be most appropriate if a similar proclamation were made here. I shall be only too happy to recommend to my colleagues that a similar course be adopted in Canada with respect to his majesty's present proclamation.
REDIVISION OF WORK OF COMMONS AND SENATE TO MEET WAR CONDITIONS On the orders of the day:

I should like to inquire of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) if the government will consider, in view of the gravity of the war and the present financial situation, appointing a committee of this house to meet Their Honours of the other chamber to consider a reallocation or redivision of the work of the two houses. The other house has adjourned for a further two weeks, and yet we have an extensive legislative programme to consider. In Washington and London the other houses are cooperating and doing a great deal in connection with war work. I brought up this matter in 1940, as reported on page 1918 of Hansard of that year, and before that in 1939, as reported on page 1471 of Hansard of that year. On both occasions the Prime Minister said that the matter would be given consideration.
I realize how busy the members of the government have been, but there are many learned gentlemen in the other house as well as former members of this house and I am sure that that house could relieve the Commons of a lot of work. Last session the other house could have handled the questions having to do with subversive elements and enemy propaganda and all that kind of thing. There are many fine members of parliament in the other place, and I ask the Prime Minister to consider this matter and give us a reply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question asked by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has been asked on previous occasions by himself. As he said, I previously replied that the government would carefully consider the matter to which he has referred. The government has considered this matter repeatedly. The leader of the government in the senate has brought up the subject time and again in meetings of the cabinet. He did so only a few days ago with regard to the work of the present session. The answer which I have just given to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) as to the legislative programme for this session answers at least in part the question the hon. member has asked. The important measures to be considered this session are all financial measures, the War Appropriation Act, the budget and supply, and in the nature of things all of these measures must originate in this house. They cannot reach the senate until this house has disposed of them.
If there were other measures contemplated I would say that the government might consider having them introduced in the senate, unless there was some special reason why they should first be introduced here. For this session the government is refraining from bringing down many measures which ordinarily we would wish to bring down simply because we desire to have the attention of the house concentrated as exclusively as possible on matters pertaining immediately to the war.
There is nothing to prevent the Senate taking any course with respect to its own proceedings which it may deem advisable. I agree with the statement of my hon. friend that there is great talent in the membership of the other house, but it is for the hon. members there to control their own business and to decide in what way they can through their membership render the greatest service to the war effort. My hon. friend has suggested a conference between the members of the two houses. I doubt that that method of procedure would be helpful at this time, for the simple reason that the government itself must decide how its business can best be advanced. Having carefully reviewed the situation we have felt that for the present session at all events we must hold to the particular course outlined, without placing restrictions either on this house or on the other, in order to make the most rapid headway we can with government measures.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES

speechtext: Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved the second reading of Bill No. 17, to amend the Pension Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the motion carries would the minister be good enough to make a statement covering the whole bill- this is by way of a question-and is it his intention to refer the bill to a committee? I think he said so the other day, but I should like to have that made clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
I did make a statement on the first reading with reference to the general principles of the bill and stated then that it was the intention immediately after the second reading to refer the bill to the special committee of the house which was appointed the other day.
In general the amendments contained in the bill place in statutory form certain orders in council which have been passed by the government during the last twelve or fourteen months. There are also certain changes with reference to administration and with reference to Canadians serving in the imperial forces, and other changes of minor importance. Every section of the bill will be carefully examined
by the special committee of the house; therefore I do not think it is necessary at this stage, when we are concerned with the general principles of the bill, to make any further explanation.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Pensions and National Health has just stated that it is the intention of the government to refer this bill to the special committee which was appointed the other day to consider questions of interest to ex-service men. If Bill No. 17 were merely a bill containing more or less routine amendments to the Canadian pension law, perhaps there would be no need to discuss it further at this stage. But it is of more importance than that, of more importance than the minister himself has just indicated, because it lays down principles to be followed in the treatment of men of the new fighting forces who suffer disability, and the principles to be followed in the treatment of their dependents.
The approach to this whole question on the part of the Canadian people and the members of this house certainly is that at least as much consideration as the men of the last war received should be shown to the men who are serving in the present fighting forces of Canada; and that any changes in the Pension Act should be of a type which will give these new soldiers, airmen and sailors at least as' much consideration as the fighting forces of * the old war have received at the hands of different parliaments of Canada.
I was astonished, on receiving this bill yesterday for the first time, to find that, while in some respects it gives additional consideration to our fighting forces, in most respects it restricts their rights. It is tightening up not only on the soldiers of the last war but on the men who are in the fighting forces at the present time. To me it smacks of officialdom. Throughout it I can see in different sections the deft touch of departmental officials, and I think that the house should realize that fact before this bill is sent to committee. I propose to-day to give several instances supporting the statement I have made.
For example, if hon. members will look at page 5 of the bill, at the top of the page they will find subsection 2 of section 11 of the Pension Act. The amendment is a departure in Canadian pension law, something entirely new, and something which restricts in a great degree the rights of these fighting men. It provides that men serving in Canada cannot receive pension for disability, nor can their dependents receive pension in the event of their death, unless the injury or disease "arose out of and was directly connected with such military or war service." In practice this
Pension Act-Mr. Green

means that it is almost impossible for a member of our forces who is serving in Canada, not having yet got overseas, or his dependents, to obtain a pension, because it must be shown that the injury or the disease was caused directly by the service; it must have been directly connected with the performance of military duties. The proof of my statement is found in the small number of men who have been able to receive pension. The minister told us the other day that 10,829 men of Canada's fighting forces, exclusive of the air force-for which he promised to get me the figures; I do not know whether they are yet'available-have been discharged from the fighting forces as physically unfit, and of that number only 484 have been able to establish claim for pension. This includes, of course, dependents receiving pension in the case of the death of the fighting man. That works out at a percentage of about 4-4 of the number of men who have been discharged as medically unfit. In other words, only 9 men in every 200 have been able to qualify for pension. This is largely because of this restrictive provision which we now find in the Pension Act and which has been used, in the shape of an order in council, for the last nine or ten months.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
What about the fifty-four
4 soldiers who have been killed on the highways by hit-and-run drivers?

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
I will leave my hon. friend to deal with that. He has spoken of it before, and spoken very well.
This situation shows that there is something wrong with the pension provision for men serving in Canada. They have been given a far more thorough medical examination than recruits in the last war, and yet we find that only 4-4 of those discharged as medically unfit are able to qualify for pension. I suggest to the house that this change in the basis of awarding pensions to Canada's fighting forces must be given careful consideration, because if we carry on under the new provision which the government now proposes, great hardship will be suffered, as the years go on, by the men who are disabled in the fighting forces and by their dependents.
Another instance of restricting the rights of the men in the forces will be found on the same page of this bill, in section 7, which enacts a new section 13 of the Pension Act. That section deals with what we call the dead-line. Hitherto, at least since the special committee met in 1936, the position has been that if a man served in the last war in Canada or England only, he or his dependents could not apply for a pension after the first day of July, 1936. There was a further provision

that, in the case of a man who served in an actual theatre of war, application could be made up to the first day of January, 1942. Originally, I believe, the date was January 1, 1940, but it has been extended until now it stands at the first of January, 1942. Time and again returned soldier members in this house have asked that the government remove that dead-line entirely, so that a man who served in a theatre of war would be able to apply for a pension whenever he broke down, regardless of whether it was before or after the first day of January, 1942. One reason for the demand was that thousands and thousands of Canadian soldiers who were wounded in the last war are not yet in receipt of pension; as they grow older many of them break down, and it was felt that there should not be a dead-line with respect to applications by such men. However, the government insisted that the dead-line stand as the first of January, 1942, and now, in this bill, the dead-line remains at that date.
The provision regarding men of the new fighting forces is even more drastic. It will be found on page 6; it provides that in the case of a man serving in the present war, no application for pension will be received after seven years from the date of his discharge. If that same provision had been in the Pension Act after the last war, men would have been cut off in 1925; under this provision, seven years after a man is discharged he will be out of luck, he will not be able to apply for a pension. There is not even a proviso to that subsection such as partly protects the man who served in an actual theatre of war in the last war; in his case the pension commission have discretion to hear the application after the dead-line is reached, but tinder this new provision for the men of the present fighting forces, the pension commission have no discretion to grant such special leave.
This new provision is copied from the pension legislation of Great Britian. As every member of this house who has had anything to do with returned soldier problems knows, the British are far more strict in their pension laws. It has been a great deal more difficult to get a pension there than in Canada. They have many more men to consider, men scattered all over the empire, and they have been hard-boiled in dealing with their veterans. Under this section the Canadian government proposes to be just as hard-boiled, and that, I suggest, is contrary to the wish of the Canadian people, contrary to the wish of the members of this house. It should not be embodied in our pension legislation.
Another example of hedging in these men will be found in the treatment of widows under this amending bill. Hon. members will

Pension Act-Mr. Green
12S3
find it at page 11 of the bill. There has been, a demand from all parts of Canada during the last few years for an extension of pensions to various classes of widows, and I think a great deal can be said in support of the contention that these women should be receiving more consideration. But we find that there is nothing in this bill to give them that further consideration. There is no extension whatever of their rights; and as for the widows of men who lose their lives in the present war, they are further restricted in that they can get a pension under the provisions of section 16 of the bill only if they -were married to the pensioner before he was granted a pension. Otherwise they cannot qualify. That is a narrower clause than we have in our Pension Act as it stands at present.
There is also a good example of tightening up on the part of departmental officials to be seen in subsection 4 on page 11 of the bill, where it is provided that if a woman has been separated from her husband she can get a pension upon his death only if she has been receiving alimony. Previously the law said, if she had been awarded alimony. There are many cases in our courts in which a woman is awarded alimony but does not receive it. In other words, she gets judgment but cannot collect. This section has been changed so that although she may have been awarded alimony she cannot get a pension on her husband's death unless she has been actually receiving it. It is an example of departmental tightening up.
At the bottom of page 11 there is the provision dealing with pension to a widow whose husband has died of his pensionable disability. At the present time the widow of a pensioner who was wounded in the last war can get that pension provided she was married before he was granted pension or before the first of January 1930, which of course was twelve years after the war. Under this bill the widow of a member of our new fighting forces cannot get the pension unless she was married to the pensioner at the time he was granted pension; in other words, no provision is made for the case of marriage within a period of years after the war.
The sum and substance of the provisions for the widow of a pensioner is this, that if the pensioner marries after he has been granted pension and then dies, upon his death his widow will be cut off. The result will be that in a few years' time there will be hundreds of widows of men now serving in our fighting forces coming to us and asking for more consideration and they will be quite right in doing so. Provision should be made for them
in this bill. At any rate, discretion should be given to the pension commission to award a pension to the widow even though she was married to the veteran after he had received his pension.
Another restriction has reference to the wife. From time to time each one of us gets complaints about these cases, and as hon. members know, there is no allowance payable for the wife of a soldier who served in the last war, if they were married after May 1, 1933. That was introduced in 1933 as an economy measure. It was unjust at that time but it has been continued ever since. Complaints have been made in the house but nothing could be done about it. The bill introduces a provision, to be found at page 16, that unless the new soldier and his wife have been married within a period of ten years after the termination of the war no allowance will be paid for the wife. There is the same restriction with respect to children. In other words, the children of our fighting forces who are lucky enough to be born within ten years of the war will receive an allowance. Any children born after that date will not. That is unfair. There is no reason for it. All the children of a pensioner should be entitled to the allowance, and none should be cut off at a date which is arbitrarily set.
This morning I had a letter from a veteran of the last war living in Manitoba, in the riding of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward). He says:
Can there not be some provision made so that an honest man can be provided for to the end that all married pensioners or veterans are afforded the same benefits of the pension act?
There is another restriction to be made in the act in the change that is being brought about in the appeal board. Hon. members will find it at page 15 of the bill. When soldier questions were considered by the special committee in 1936, the veteran at that time had the right to apply first of all to the pension commission, then to be heard by a quorum of two members of the pension commission-they sat in different parts of the country, saw the man and heard evidence- and finally he had the right of appeal to the pension appeal court, sitting in Ottawa and consisting of three men. Subsequently that was changed and to-day the veteran applying for a pension has the right, first of all, to what is called a first hearing, which is really not a hearing at all but a first consideration by the pension commission in Ottawa-all done by correspondence. Then, if his application is rejected, he has the right to a second hearing, which again is merely consideration given at Ottawa. Then he has the right of final appeal, to an appeal board, which sits in different parts of the country, for example in
Pension Act-Mr. Turgeon

Halifax or Vancouver. The veteran can go before that board of three men, take his witnesses with him and have a proper hearing; and he derives great satisfaction from being able to tell his story to those three men. Now under section 22 of this bill the government proposes to cut that final appeal board down from three men to two; and section 23 goes on to provide that in case of a split verdict, in case one member of the new board is for the soldier and one against him, the decision will be made by a man sitting here in Ottawa, a commissioner appointed by the chairman of the pension commission.

speechtext: Who did not hear the appeal or see the witnesses.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
Who did not hear the witnesses at all and did not hear the ex-serviceman's story, but who sits here in Ottawa and looks through a file. That is not good enough. Certainly it is one of the provisions of the bill which should not be retained. Nothing will do more to stir up the veterans across the country than to have some man here in Ottawa given the power to throw out their application for pension on a final appeal.
There are some provisions of the bill which are helpful. One in particular will be found on page 13: I refer to the provision for extending the Pension Act to cover Canadians who serve in the Royal Air Force or the Royal Navy. But it also is too restricted. The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone), when the resolution which preceded this bill was under consideration, brought out the fact that those young Canadians who enlisted in the Royal Air Force before the war broke out cannot get pensions under the -act. Under these amendments the only airmen who can benefit are those who have enlisted in the Royal Air Force since the war started; it does not cover those who went to England in 1939 or 1938, or the other years preceding the war. I suggest that the bill should be extended to cover those eases.
I mention these instances in the hope that consideration will be given to them not only by hon. members who happen to be on this special committee but also by all other hon. members. I say that this bill is fundamentally wrong, because the whole tendency is to be tough," to be just a little tougher than before on the men in the fighting forces. That means that if parliament enacts this bill in its present shape it will be "tough" with the very Canadians who should be receiving the most consideration at the present time. .

speechtext:
With some of the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) I am in agreement. I refer especially to the sections of the bill which deal with widows, and to certain features of section 5 with regard to men injured in service after May 21 last.
It is not my intention to deal with these matters now on the motion for second reading, because I think they can best be discussed in the special committee that has been set up. After the bill returns from the committee with any recommended amendments, the house can better deal with it.
I think this country is fortunate in having as minister in charge of pensions one who for many years before he came to this parliament was dealing with the matter of pensions on behalf of soldiers, or their wives and dependents, because of injuries received during the war. I commend this bill, on general principles, to the house, on the understanding of course that favourable consideration will be given to any amendments which may be proposed by the special committee.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
In view of the fact that a special committee has been appointed to go into this question it may appear to be a waste of time to discuss just now the matters brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). I do wish, however, to take this opportunity of saying that I have had some experience with pension matters during the past twenty years and I am entirely in agreement with the statements just made by that hon. member. There is no need for me to repeat what the hon. member has said. I agree that the select committee will have a certain duty to perform, but the bill contains certain provisions and principles with which I am not in agreement, and if it is given second reading as it stands and goes to the special committee, we can be reasonably sure that it will come back in the same form.
I see the bill in this light, that it is an indication of the considered policy of the government as to the manner in which pensions should be dealt with at the present time; and the committee will naturally be guided by the Minister of Pensions and National Health. In addition, the members of the government party constitute a majority of the committee.
I am assuming that the bill embodies the policy of the government, otherwise it would not be here in this form; it is reasonable therefore to suppose that that is exactly what will come out. What I am concerned with at the moment is that it is clearly shown by the amendments that the insurance principle, or "incurred during service" principle, is being

Pension Act-Mr. Gillis
practically eliminated in several clauses, and that the man who enlists for service in Canada only is discriminated against. In the last war the man who saw service in Canada only was included in the pension provisions and had exactly the same opportunity to qualify as the man who served overseas, if he incurred a disability while on military service. The bill as amended very definitely sets out in clause after clause, and underlines it, that the disability must have been incurred on war service. The trainees who are being called up at the present time find themselves in this position: They have the option of volunteering for service overseas. Many perhaps will not feel inclined to volunteer; they may believe that their service can be better rendered in this country. As the bill stands it may be construed as a lever to induce a man to volunteer for overseas service. This principle, the insurance principle or "incurred on service" principle, was dealt with exhaustively in 1921 under a commission headed by the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). After considerable inquiry by that commission it was held in 1921 that the original intention of parliament was to protect all members of the forces w'ith respect to any injury or disease incurred during the period that they wore the king's uniform. Those with service in Canada only received the benefit of this protection during the great war. There is no valid reason why any discrimination should now' be introduced against those who serve in Canada only.
There are many things I should like to see included in the bill. Among all the grievances with regard to pensions which in the past twenty years have been aired there is one which, in my opinion, should receive special consideration in the bill before the house. I refer to the service of nursing sisters. In the last few months I have carried on a correspondence with the Department of Pensions and National Health concerning a nursing sister who saw service in Prance from 1917 to 1919. To-day, completely disabled, she receives only a small stipend under the provision for war veterans' allowances. This sister considers herself as a recipient of charity. She feels she is entitled to a pension by virtue of her service. But because her documentation or her files are not as they should be, or because they do not agree with her version of her disability, it has been declared that she is not now eligible for pension. Arrangements have been made to have her case heard by a tribunal.
In my opinion the act should deal specially with nursing sisters. Any girl who volunteers her services to her country and serves her time in hospitals overseas, any girl who serves
in an actual theatre of war, who goes through bombing raids and all the horrors connected with surgical operations performed under difficult circumstances in military hospitals, regardless of whether she has been actually wounded or seriously ill, in my opinion suffers shock to her nervous system. The fact that she has gone through a couple of years of that kind of life has left its mark on her. The fact that she volunteered her services and actually served in a theatre of war should entitle her to pension, regardless of whether or not she has the required documentation. The fact that she did her work and that she is not now in a position to earn a livelihood ought to be sufficient to entitle her to the pension. Many of the women who served during the last war sacrificed practically everything that a woman values in life. Many of them continued their services in military hospitals after the war. Many of them never married. Specific provision should be made in the Pension Act for women who render service of this kind.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health will recall that about a month ago I wrote him respecting a man who had gone from Sydney, Nova Scotia, to England, on a convoy ship, leaving a family in Glace Bay. Shortly after landing at Liverpool he was killed during a bombing raid on that city, and his wife was left destitute. The landlord threatened to throw her out on the street. I went to see her; she explained the circumstances, and I telegraphed the minister. Let me say right here that the minister acted promptly, and did everything he could, within the regulations. But in my opinion because of those regulations that woman is suffering hardship.
The minister explained to me that any man serving on a convoy ship of Canadian registry is protected by the Pension Act, and that under these circumstances there would be no difficulty in obtaining a pension. The procedure of convoying is undoubtedly one of the most essential in our war services at the present time. It is also very dangerous. A large percentage of the ships plying between England and Canada to-day are of British or foreign registry. Only a small minority are of Canadian registry. In the instance to which I have called attention the ship was of British registry. The minister has communicated with the British representative in Canada, and is carrying on negotiations with a view to having the woman pensioned. However, this condition developed two months ago, and the woman is now receiving relief from the city. So far there has not been any pension adjustment. In my opinion it is not fair to those
Pension Act-Mr. Gillis

who are suffering that they should have to depend on the British government, under present circumstances, to take care of such cases. While I have mentioned only one, we know that more may arise at any time. Regardless of a ship's registry, any Canadian operating on a convoy from a Canadian port should receive the protection of the Canadian government, and his dependents should be in a similar position. This is not a British war; it is an empire war, and we are all engaged in it. The government of Canada should accept the responsibility of caring for the dependents of men who have been fatally injured in any phase of our war effort.
I know the minister has been working in the matter. He has done all he can toward making an adjustment, under present regulations. But in order to take care of matters of that kind the regulations should be extended. As the hon. member for Vancouver South pointed out, there are many widows in Canada to-day. Petition after petition, resolution after resolution come to us every day from different organizations asking that the regulations be extended to take care of the widows of exservice men who cannot now be provided; for.
Any man who went through the last war will agree that practically all who came back after being in the line for any considerable time returned with a certain percentage of disability. The life of any man who was in the line was shortened because of his service there. Many are widows to-day because their husbands are in premature graves. Had the proper documentation been on record, many of them would be eligible for pension. But we know that during the first year or two of the war in France records were not kept as scrupulously as they should have been, and as a result many men have been denied their right to pension.
I should like to see a provision in this measure which would take care of the situation I have described. With all due respect, I am reasonably sure the committee will recommend what is in the minds of the sponsors of the bill. We may go into committee, talk, make recommendations and all the rest of it; nevertheless I do not believe that in any material respect the bill will be changed. I should like to have the principle to which I have referred understood by hon. members before deliberations by the committee take place.
Every man who puts on the king's uniform, and who is on military service, engaged in the war effort, should receive the protection of the state while he is wearing that uniform. This is a classic example of what might happen under the legislation as it now stands. A

man who meets with an accident while on leave, and not connected with his military duties, oannot claim pension. For example, let us suppose that the leader of the opposition and I are in the same unit. I am going on leave, and I am not subject to the performance of military duty while I am on leave. The leader of the opposition, we will suppose, is driving me to the station. There is an accident and we are both killed. The widow of the leader of the opposition would be entitled to pension, and mine would not.. Because I was off duty and going on leave, my wife and dependents would be deprived of pension, under the regulations as I understand them. This is a condition which should not exist. While one is wearing the king's uniform he and his dependents should be entitled to the protection of the state. Many things may happen to one who is on service which may not happen to one who is not on service.
I am interested in this matter because in the past I have had some experience with pensions. At the moment that is all I have to say.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my view a number of the matters brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) should receive most careful study in committee. I am not a member of the committee and in my view this is not the time to go into details, particularly since my colleague, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Turgeon), has expressed to the house the exact views, which I entertain in regard to this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that this bill is very restrictive in its nature. I think there will have to be a few changes made when it is in committee.
Another point which I should like, to bring to the attention of the house is this. I refer to a principle which is being carried forward from the old act. At this time I think we should have an equalization of pensions. Under *the old act, men with the rank of lieutenant or under receive $900 for a total disability, while a brigadier-general receives $2,700 for a total disability. The widow of a man of the rank of lieutenant or under receives $720 while the widow of a brigadier-general receives $2,160.
This war is entirely different from the last war. Our forces have been highly mechanized and many of the non-commissioned officers and other ranks must have mechanical exper-

Pension Act-Mr. Wright
ience. I believe such men are entitled to a pension equal to that paid to 'higher ranks. This principle was agreed to by the former Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) in 1936. A question was asked with regard to hospitalization and the then minister replied as follows:
That is to say, a private soldier was placed on pay and allowances approximately equal to those which he received as a private soldier in the army, and a general or colonel was placed on the pay and allowances of the rank which he held in the army. The divergence has always appeared to me to be pretty wide, and after considerable study the officers of the department and myself came to the conclusion that perhaps at this time, twenty years after the war, we should not perpetuate the system of pay according to rank which existed during the war.
This difference in pensions paid to the different ranks was a carryover from the British system. I believe we could very well change the legislation to provide an equalization of pensions to all members of the forces.
I do not mean that there should be a reduction in the total amount paid, because the saving achieved could be used to raise the schedule of the lower pensions. A pension of $900 for total disability is quite small. The cost of living in this country has been rising continually and will continue to go up after this war. This is something which the house should decide and give instructions accordingly to the committee. Most of those from the higher ranks go into protected occupations after serving where their disabilities are not of as great disadvantage as similar disabilities suffered by men who have served in the lower ranks. For instance, a man who is a bricklayer by trade and who loses his leg finds that disability much greater than a man who works in an office and is suffering from the same disability. We should consider seriously this matter of the equalization of pensions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this bill is to be referred to a committee I shall be very brief, especially in view of the fact that the last time we considered such a bill it was dealt with most extensively. I have no fear that we shall not be given the fullest opportunity to make what we consider to be essential amendments to this bill. If I remember correctly, we practically rewrote the last bill in committee. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) raised a number of important points. He pointed out that we were changing the whole principle of certain clauses of the act in such a way that the benefits accruing to soldiers will be restricted rather than expanded. I believe that public opinion to-day is almost unanimous in demanding that the
benefits of our pension legislation shall be expanded rather than restricted in any shape or form.
For instance, reference has been made to the fact that a soldier will not be eligible for pension unless he has been actually engaged in war service. I can visualize a man being given two or three days' leave and taking ill, or suffering some form of disability on the second day of his leave. Under this bill he would not be able to get a pension.
I do not think the people of Canada will agree with that. No provision is being made in this bill to provide pensions for the war widow whose husband does not have a 50 per cent war disability. Ever since the last war an effort has been made to obtain some consideration for these widows. We must realize that we are not fulfilling our obligations to the men in the forces until every man who enlists is assured that when he dies his widow will get whatever pension he may have been receiving.
When a man is entitled to pension, he receives a larger pension if he is married. We thereby recognize a certain responsibility for the man's wife. Yet we say that should he die we will not assume any responsibility for his widow unless he is in receipt of a pension for a fifty per cent disability or over, or unless the widow can prove that he died as a result of a war service. Five, ten or fifteen years after a war a widow may find it impossible to furnish such proof. I have no doubt that every hon. member has a file of cases in which he has been trying to get pensions for widows and has been turned down because they have not been able to furnish this proof.
I have one reason to hope that we may be able to get more for the soldiers in this committee than we were able to obtain in the last, in that while in opposition the present minister took a very broad stand on the question of money. I have read a number of statements made by him prior to 1935 in which he took a very broad view.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext: He has changed since then.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
We will have plenty of opportunity to remind him of the stand he took. There is no excuse for saying that we cannot make these payments because there is no money available. It was admitted in the last committee that it was not a question of deciding what was due to the soldier, it was simply a question of deciding how much money we had available. It was admitted freely that we were not prepared to assume our full responsibilities to the returned men because the nation was bankrupt. The word "bankrupt" was actually used. I hope a
Pension Act-Mr Ross (Souris)

similar state of affairs will not obtain in this committee. When we are spending millions upon millions of dollars daily and weekly I hope we are not going to be told that we cannot find the paltry few thousand dollars necessary for this or that because the country is bankrupt. I do not think we should expect our soldiers to make sacrifices unless we are prepared to assume the responsibility of looking after their dependents after the war. We have not taken care of their dependents, and we know it.
This bill is going to a committee and I sincerely hope we shall be given every opportunity to deal with all phases of the Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I shall not say any more at this time.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been pointed out, we expect to be given ample opportunity to discuss this bill in committee. As the previous speaker (Mr. Quelch) has said, I trust that we shall be given an opportunity to rewrite this bill to some extent, but candidly I am not as hopeful as he is in that respect.
There are two or three things I should like to point out. First I am disappointed that in framing this bill consideration has not been given to providing for war widows and for the widows of pensioners.
Secondly, I am of the opinion that provision should also have been made for the dependents of those who die on active service in Canada.
I can visualize a young man, with a young wife and a family of small children, giving up a good position to serve in our armed forces at a rate of remuneration one-third less than he received in civil life. Should he become a casualty I do not think it is fair that the whole family should become a charge on the local municipality, which in some cases would be their only recourse.
With reference to the appeal board, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), I think it is a retrograde step that we should be appointing a board of two members instead of the three that we have had in the past. In case of disagreement the case is referred for decision to a third party who has not even heard the evidence. Surely that is a retrograde step. I trust that we may have ample opportunity in committee to rectify it, as well as many other deficiencies in the bill.
Since we are going to discuss the bill in detail in committee, I shall not take up more of the time of the house now.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the great military hospitals is located in my riding, and I suppose few members of the house have more appeals made to them on behalf of veterans or their 
dependents than I have. Were there any public benefit to be gained by a discussion of this bill in detail now, I should wish to be heard extensively at this stage. But the bill is going to a committee, and the subject matter is largely one of detail rather than of general character.
Somebody has said that the people of Canada do not desire a tightening-up in this matter. I think I may say that the people of Canada desire neither the one nor the other, neither a tightening-up nor a broadening-out. If there is any public opinion at all on this matter it is that the Pension Act must be not generous, not mean, not niggardly, but just. The people of Canada are prepared to discharge their responsibilities with respect to the dependents of our soldiers abroad or in Canada, but the job of making the bill just and accurate is a job for a committee and not for the house in general. Therefore, sir, I join with others in saying that we should give the bill second reading and reserve details for discussion in the special committee.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few moments but I wish to say a few words about that small group of Canada's permanent army who retired prior to 1919 and were pensioned. In 1919 the government at Ottawa realized that in view of the increased cost of living the pensions being paid to long-service men of what was then known as the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and of the permanent army were inadequate, and accordingly the pensions to these men were increased in the neighbourhood of 500 per cent. I have spoken on this matter in the house before. I do not think it comes directly under this act, but undoubtedly something should be done about it. I am sure that a great many members have had this particular matter brought to their attention.

May I ask the hon.
gentleman a question? Does he know that I have already applied to the prospective chairman of the special committee on this bill to have the veterans heard by the committee, and that they will be coming to Ottawa to make their representations?

speechtext:
They have been asked to come to Ottawa a great many times since 1935 when they had this matter up, and they have had some very pleasant things said to them. I have here extracts from letters they have received from Ottawa, and if my hon. friend wants to get into a controversy about this thing I am ready. Here is a letter from, I think, the Minister of National Defence at that time, in which he states:
In my opinion your claim is based on complete fairness. I fully sympathize with you.

Pension Act-Mr. Hazen
12S9
Here is another letter from Mr. MacLean, of Prince Edward Island, and I have dozens more here. Here is one from the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock). They have received all these letters but nothing has been done for them, and something must be done because the present situation is unfair to them. Let me state what some of the pensions of these men are.
Here is a man getting a pension of $17.93, and the present rate of pension for a similar case would be $93.00. Here is another one receiving $17.31, and the present pension would be $66.00. Here is another one receiving $9.99, and the present pension would be $48.00. Here .is another receiving $20.60 and the present pension would be $41.81. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the house to get something done for these men. There is only a small group of them but their claims have been under consideration now for five or six years and it is time that action was taken if we are ever going to get any action at all.
There is another matter on which I wish to say something. When a soldier in Canada is on leave he is not supposed to be on duty, and if he is injured on leave he gets no pension. Under the present arrangements the only way in which many of our soldiers can travel from one place to another in Canada is by hitch-hiking. No free transportation on the railways is supplied to them, and it costs money to travel from place to place; therefore they travel in automobiles in which they seek rides. In some of the provinces, if a passenger is injured in a motor car accident he has no claim against the driver, and therefore he has no comeback. It seems to me that the government ought to do something about providing transportation for these men. Surely that could be done; or when they are on leave and travelling from one place to another, if they meet with an accident, they should be considered as being on duty. It is unfair that they should have no right to a pension if an accident happens on their weekend leave.
There is another appeal which we made in the house last year and again this year, and that is on behalf of widows. I sipoke on their behalf the other day and I wish to add a few words to-day. I think the government in this bill could very easily reduce the percentage of pensionable disability so that the widow could qualify and get her pension. These widows are all getting older and many of them are in a very bad way financially. We could take this step now quite easily, and if the government do not feel like going 14873-82
the whole way we could at least meet the claims of these widows half way so that all of these widows might get some pension.
I am not a member of the committee but I hope the committee will make a great many changes in the bill as it stands at present.

A number of important suggestions have been made this afternoon concerning this bill, all of which no doubt will be given careful consideration by the committee to which it will be referred. I am not a member of the committee, and I should like to make one or two suggestions now, in the hope that they will receive attention.
The first is that this bill include a class of men who are not mentioned in it at the present time-the men who belong to Canada's merchant marine. These men face during this war, and up to the present time have faced perhaps as great danger, and probably more, than most of our fighting forces. Some recognition should be given of their services, by including them within the provisions of this bill. It could be done by amending paragraphs (i) and (j) of section 1. I do not want to elaborate on this matter, but I hope the committee will seriously consider the inclusion of members of Canada's merchant marine who have served on the high seas.
One other suggestion I would make; it has to do with section 5 of the bill, section 11 of the old act, namely, that at the end of paragraph (a) the following words be added: "while on or off duty." The last line of the paragraph would then read:
-attributable to or was incurred during such war service, while on or off duty.
Possibly after those words there might be added: "if not disobeying orders."

I wish to say just a word or two with regard to pensions as they affect Canadian seamen. Nothing in this bill refers to Canadian seamen as such, but some time ago the government passed an order in council-a very generous order in council, I think-which says in effect that seamen and fishermen in the performance of their duties who suffer by reason of contact with the enemy shall be given the same privileges with regard to pension as are given to the active forces of the country. However, as has been brought out by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), it appears that this refers only to Canadian seamen on ships of Canadian registry. Might I point out to you, sir, and to the house, that the number of ships of Canadian registry which travel overseas or are in the overseas trade is very

Pension Act-Mr. Kinley

small indeed. Even the ships which are commonly called Canadian and operated by big Canadian companies are registered in Great Britain. The present limitation would restrict these benefits to a very small number of Canadian seamen and-what is worse-would leave out many who would be eminently qualified for pension.
I	recall that soon after the Jervis Bay went down in her fight on the Atlantic, I met a young man of my town who was a member of that crew. A great many seamen along the coast of Nova Scotia are on oil tankers and on ships of every register. We must recognize that service upon the sea is a common service to all countries. Whether you are on a British ship or some other ship, you are still working for the cause of the empire; it is, as it were, a universal service which extends beyond the boundaries of any one country. Furthermore, those who were so anxious to serve that they joined a foreign ship or a ship outside of Canadian registry are in most cases serving aboard an empire ship; for do not forget that the shipping of Norway, the Netherlands and some other countries is controlled by our own empire, so that these men in reality are working under the direction of the central authority of the empire that is carrying on this war. It will cause a great deal of trouble and much suffering in my part of the country if these brave Canadians who are serving on ships on the high seas are debarred from the privilege of receiving pension from the country which they so well serve.
I am not a member of this committee, but I hope that the minister, and through him the government, will see to it that the generous treatment which they have accorded to seamen-a new departure in the statutes of this country-will be further amplified in the direction I have mentioned. Such treatment will be well deserved, arid will acknowledge a service which is most vital at the present time, when a Macedonian cry has gone out for more ships, a call by the head of the British empire. We must have crews 'to man those ships, and those men must have the very best treatment we can give them.

I make the statement in all sincerity after an experience of something like sixteen and a half 5'ears with ex-service men's affairs.

I do not think the statement of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) should be misunderstood, or the attitude he took. It is generally understood that when a bill is given second reading, it means that we are accepting the principle; and while the committee who will take this bill under consideration have it within their power to suggest changes and amendments, the general principle contained in the bill will remain after it has been given its second reading in this house.
In our view that should not be the situation, because there are embodied in this bill principles which we believe should not be accepted. Not only the details and terms of the bill but also some of the principles ought to be referred to the committee. We have particular reference to the removal of the principle of insurance. Up to the present time it has been understood that from the time a man donned the king's uniform until he was demobilized he was insured with regard to becoming disabled or being killed, that there was definite protection for himself and for his dependents should anything happen to him, irrespective of where or how it happened. What we are proposing to do under this bill is, as I understand it, to draw a line, by which,
1292	COMMONS
Pension Act-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
if his accident happens in Canada, a man will have to show, or his widow will have to show in the event of his death, that his injury came about as the result of his military duty. That is going to raise a great many difficult points, and there will be many borderline cases.
I have in mind a young man who was in the active service force for something over a year; he joined in September, 1939, and was discharged in December, 1940. He was fit and a good soldier. He slipped while taking a shower bath, fell and injured his spine. He was brought back to Weybum and discharged with a month's pay. What is that man's position under this legislation? In this particular case the returned men in the district rallied round him and he was given a job in the local mental hospital, and has been able to support himself and his family.
But multiply that case by many hundreds that we are bound to have, and the department will find itself faced with innumerable difficulties. This bill does away with the covering principle of insurance and the sense of security of men in uniform. The committee should give this matter serious consideration. There may be many cases like the one I have mentioned, and that is not good advertising. Young men contemplating entering the service, particularly married men with dependents, are going to view with some trepidation the removal of the insurance principle and the bringing in of a principle which requires a man to show that his injury, or his widow to show that his death, was directly due to his military service. What the hon. member for Cape Breton South had in mind is, I think, valid, that in allowing this bill to go to the committee we are not accepting the principle of removing the insurance principle that has always existed, but we want the committee to give the matter most careful consideration and, if possible, bring in something more satisfactory.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OP CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext:
To all realistic, right-minded people this bill is positively disgusting. The principle of the bill is the principle of scarcity, under which we have worked for a hundred years. It is a niggardly, cheese-paring and restrictive measure. This government asks for a total war; it asks the people to give their all. The risks involved are tremendous. Surely the government ought to be prepared to take the risk along with the men and their wives and children. This bill is conceived and modelled in the atmosphere of reaction; it looks backward instead of forward. It ignores two fundamental facts. The first is that what is physically possible must be made financially 
possible; if not in this generation of blindness and lack of vision, it must in the next generation. The second fact ignored is that we are progressing into an age which will be even more an age of plenty than that in which we now live; consequently there will be more unemployment, fewer markets, heavier taxation, greater restrictions on everyone engaged in an effort to make a living. If it was next to impossible for men to make a living before they joined the forces; if they had to be content with meagre pittances such as $7.50 a month for working on a farm, how on earth are they going to support themselves when they come back from this war?
There is plenty of money to equip these men for war. There must be found money to support them as well as their dependents after the war. There are at the present time many widows of soldiers who fought in the last war who cannot get work. They are efficient women, capable of doing good work. I could name one here in Ottawa who is thoroughly qualified to take as fine a position as can be found in the civil service, and that woman cannot even get a hearing. She is only one of thousands. Nevertheless we have ministers of the crown prating about lack of men and lack of help in this country. It is disgusting. It is disgraceful. As long as we allow ourselves to be hoodwinked by such plausibility, such specious reasoning, we are unfit for the positions we hold.
There are in Canada veterans by the ten thousand who cannot get work, not because they are not qualified but because they happen to be a few years too old. What is going to be the situation twenty or thirty or forty years from now? Surely we are not going to ask people rising out of the mire of misery and poverty to risk their all, to fall back afterwards into a similar mire. There are in this country returned men's children 'by the ten thousand who can get no work. Under provincial laws, when a widow's child becomes fifteen or sixteen years of age the widow's allowance is cut off, the assumption apparently being that a child of fifteen or sixteen can immediately get work and thereby contribute to the support of the family. Under the present circumstances that is utterly absurd, and every hon. member knows it. Then why not face facts as they are?
To-day there are countless returned men engaged in production who cannot sell their product for enough to yield them a living. We have farmers by the ten thousand-not all are returned men but many are-who are in that state. There are thousands of manufacturers; tens of thousands of tradesmen, such as carpenters, blacksmiths, builders of

Pension Act-Mr. Blackmore
various kinds; thousands of professional men, such as lawyers, doctors, teachers and the like, returned men, who cannot by any possible means make enough to support themselves in a decent, respectable manner. They are on the verge of bankruptcy all the time. Yet this bill is apparently designed to perpetuate these abominations into the next generation. When one considers the number of provinces in this dominion which put such licence restrictions around men that it is virtually impossible for a tradesman to go out and get work, unless he happens to be able to qualify for a licence, utterly disregarding the possibility of the man's making a living, in the event of his not being able to get work at his trade, it is a disgrace to the house and to the country that in the presence of such a situation we calmly contemplate a measure like this.
If the condition has been so bad up to the present time, then I ask any hon. member: What do you suppose it will be when the men come back? Let us be realistic. Why not give a pension to all the men who go into the forces, all the men who serve? Why not remove them from the competition in work and production, unless they choose to go into that competition? This thought may startle people, but there has to be something that will startle people, something widely different from anything which has been conceived in high places thus far, and widely different from anything which has been made to prevail in this country thus far.
The question we need to ask ourselves is this: Is this Canada of ours able to produce enough food, enough clothes, enough shelter, enough education, enough culture and enough recreation to provide for the men who don the king's uniform, both while they are in that uniform and afterwards, with all the food, clothing, shelter, education, culture, and recreation they need? If that question is asked, then the answer simply must be yes. I would defy any man in this house successfully to controvert that statement.
If then it is physically possible-and it is going to be physically possible, provided we are able to defend this land

to give those men the standard of living we all know they ought to have, then why not seriously contemplate it now?
After the war we should be able to do a great deal better than we are doing to-day. If it is possible for us to produce all these goods now, what will be the condition after the war? I ask this: What are we going to do with this great amount of bacon we now are gearing ourselves to produce and to supply to Great Britain, when no longer the British
people are able to take it, or when they are able to produce their own? What are we going to do with the butter, the cheese and the great amount of clothing we are now enabling ourselves to produce? Are we going to stop producing them, and let men suffer? What a piece of monstrous nonsense even to think ofl What are we going to do with the great amount of manufacturing power we are building up in the production of ammunition? Are we going to dismantle the ammunition plants, and turn the men on the streets, saying to them, "We have no further need for you; go and ride the rods"? Are we going to tell them, "Go out into your cities and go on relief, so that the municipalities may keep you"? Why in the name of common sense can we not put those men to work producing food, clothing, shelter and other things, and distributing them among the people of Canada, and thus give the returned men something like a proper standard of living?
What are we going to do about the many devices being perfected during this war to speed up production? What are we going to do with the aeroplanes we shall have in such great abundance when the war is over? Are we going to use them for the betterment of our people? Are we going to use them for the betterment of the people of the world, or are we going to take them out and scrap them? Can any one contemplate the latter proposal with equanimity? If we are going to use them, then we are going to use them for some purpose of production. What are we going to do with the production? We must set ourselves to discover a new system, a new economic order, which will enable us to distribute our goods among our people. Once that is done we shall never have any more worry about supplying men with a fair standard of living. If this government cannot discover a system of distribution, then I say shame on the government, shame on every single man who occupies a cabinet position and shame on every man who sits in support of it.

This bill is a digrace to Canada. It is an insult to this house. Every member is ashamed of it. I know that, from talking with the members individually; I know the attitude they take. They are just as anxious as I am to see the returned men have a fair chance; that means they must be ashamed of this bill.
Pension Act-Mr. White

Every private member, every minister, must be mortified to contemplate this bill. If the government could not do better thani present legislation such as that we now have before us, then let everyone in Canada know it, and know it now.
Let us in this house, all of us, sir, be worthy of the trust conferred upon us. Let us for once not betray Canada. Let us demand what we want. Let us be realistic. Let us decide what is physically possible in Canada, and then let us insist on what is physically possible being made financially possible, for our fighting forces.
If the present financial system be such that it must say it cannot be done, that system thereby declares its own condemnation, insufficiency, impotence, and ineptitude. It gives notice that it is no longer worthy of the respect of any intelligent community. I ask the committee to give us a bill fit to appear in a modem British legislature. I then ask the house to demand that the government make the implementation of that bill possible.

Mr. Speaker, I should like, first, to deal with the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). He brought out many valuable suggestions with which I am sure the committee will deal fully. I should like, too, to associate myself with the observation of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) to the effect that, after the bill is passed-and I think it will be a fine one when it is completed, despite the violent speech of the previous speaker-in the administration of the act, over which we as members will have no control, there should be on the board at least one man who during the war served as a private soldier.
At the last session the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) laid down the principle that all future officers in the army must come from the ranks, thereby indicating that at this late date the army recognizes the fact that the most efficient officer must come from the ranks because of his first having served as a private, having become a non-commissioned officer and having later on been promoted to the rank of an officer. Every officer who began service as a private and then served as a non-commissioned officer always understands the private's point of view. One of the great faults in connection with the administration of the Pension Act is that practically all who are in charge-doctors and other officials -never served as privates or non-commissioned officers, and therefore do not understand the viewpoint of the private soldier.
I have dealt with the pension board for twenty years. Since this war began, a battalion left

from my riding for overseas. Quite a number of men have been returned home because of illness or injuries received through bombings and things of that kind. I have made various applications to the pension board and I regret to say that, despite what the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has said, I have received little satisfaction, the board is already tough; quite frequently a letter comes back with two excuses: first, that the injury complained of is not due to military service and, second, that the injury complained of has not been aggravated by military service. Yet in 1939 these men passed a strict examination by a board of three doctors. They were X-rayed and accepted in category A. They went to England and within a few months or a year were returned home and placed in category D or E. Yet these men cannot obtain pensions. That is why I agree with the hon. member for New Westminster when he says that it is in the administration of the Pension Act that we are perhaps falling down.
Unfortunately, when a private soldier or a non-commissioned officer goes to the pension board, he finds that there still clings to that board a trace of the old military discipline. A distinction is made between the private and the officer. I should like to outline one case briefly. This occurred two years ago in my riding. This man, a private soldier, suffered a recurrence of a serious wound which he had received over twenty years ago. The local medical doctor in the pension department sent the man to the Kingston general hospital, where a small number of rooms are reserved for military patients. He was attended by one of the leading physicians in Kingston; he was dangerously ill and it was a question whether he would live. The doctor in charge gave instructions that he should be placed in a private room and be provided with a private nurse because he was delirious much of the time. He was moved to a private room and furnished with a private nurse, but when it caime time to pay for this service he found that he had to pay the money out of his own pocket. The total amount paid to the Kingston hospital was $79.50.
I took up the matter with the pension board, and the administrator told me himself -this is not hearsay-that under the regulations as they stood at that date there was no provision for a private soldier to be furnished with a private room in a hospital and a private nurse. I asked him if he considered that a private soldier was not of sufficient importance to Canada to be entitled to a private nurse when his life was in danger, but the administrator said that he

Pension Act-Mr. Mackenzie
was sorry, the regulations contained no provision for that. To date that man has never been reimbursed for the money he paid to the hospital. The disability from which he suffered was 100 per cent due to the effects of his war wound. We may pass the finest act under the sun and yet have it fall down in administration. If we had a few private soldiers active in the administration of this legislation, much of the present trouble would disappear.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): Mr. Speaker,
I think the house will generally agree that we have had a most vigorous debate upon the second reading of this bill. I am not going to endeavour to reply to the extremely extravagant, and to my mind unjustifiable language used by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) with regard to this measure. I venture to suggest to my hon. friend that he has not given a wide study to the terms of this bill. If he had, he would have been more conscious of his definite responsibility as a member of this house than to use such extreme and extravagant language.
As I said the other day, there is a tradition in this house with regard to measures dealing with pensions. In days gone by, that tradition has always enabled the house to deal with such measures on a strictly non-partisan basis. During the course of this debate many hon. members seem to have forgotten the terms of reference to the select committee which was agreed to the other day by this house. Not only is this particular measure to be referred to that select committee, but the general provisions of our pension legislation as well as the War Veterans' Allowance Act are also referred to the committee. That committee will have complete jurisdiction, not only to consider and pass upon the adequacy or otherwise of the present measure, but to discuss other provisions of the Pension Act or phases of the pension administration. If hon. members had been mindful and conscious of that fact during the course of this debate, many of the statements which were made would not have been made.
I can say that it was not necessary for the government to introduce this bill at this time, from the point of view either of authority or of administration. We could have functioned until the end of this war. As a matter of fact, it was thought better that this bill should be submitted or that the basic principle should be submitted to the attention of parliament at this time so that a free and unfettered judgment could be passed thereon. Could
anything be more fair than that? Yet the hon. member for Lethbridge uses the words "disgraceful and disgusting."

May I assure my hon. friend that we are doing nothing of the kind. If there is objection to that section, I shall have no hesitation in having it removed. An attempt is being made to make the period of service in another body count as service under the terms of the Pension Act in qualifying a man for pension. If there is objection to that section, let us strike it out. Not a single right is taken away from anyone by this bill.
With reference to the points that have been raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, every one of them was discussed in years gone by in other committees of this house and every one of them was rejected.
With regard to those serving in the present war, a committee has been set up to consider this very question of service within Canada as against outside. An important question of principle is involved. It is, I might say, the only important question involved in this measure, apart from the extended benefits that are given to every Canadian serving with the imperial forces. That question will be thoroughly discussed by the committee. I can assure my hon. friend that no restrictions whatsoever will be placed on the committee's deliberations. There will be the fullest, freest, frankest discussion of the Pension Act generally, of war veteran allowances generally, and of all other measures which are necessary to effect a real rehabilitation of our ex-service men.
May I suggest in closing, Mr. Speaker, from what I have seen of the committee, that I know the spirit of the committee will be better than that which has been displayed by some members of the house this 
afternoon. I am sure the committee will meet in a spirit of cooperation and helpfulness and with an earnest desire to bring back into this house a measure which will do justice and fairness to our men who are doing so much not only for Canada but for the empire, the world and Christianity itself at the present time.
