subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since I started to discuss the matter of aircraft production, events have happened which have made great changes in Europe and brought home to us the fury that may well sweep over Europe within the next few weeks. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said this afternoon that, so far as he knew at the present time, this session would be devoted in the main to a discussion of the war appropriation bill and the budget, that all our ideas would be directed to one matter, that of winning the war.
The attitude which we on this side of the house take is that we owe it as a duty to those whom we represent to do everything we can at this time and during this discussion to remove the veil of secrecy which to-day conceals from any of our people the gravity of the situation in this country and in the empire. Apathy must be swept aside because for too many people in this dominion the war is yet but a daily radio programme of changing events.

War Appropriation Bill
The attitude we take on this side of the house is that one of the things that will be of paramount importance in determining the outcome of this war is air power and aircraft production. We have heard from the Prime Minister himself that Canada's contribution to the air training scheme may well be the determining and decisive factor in this war. Churchill has called for planes, and still more planes.
I make these explanations for the reason that they accord me an opportunity of saying why I intend to devote some time this afternoon to a discussion of the speech delivered the other day by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and to the MacMillan report, and also to a discussion of the Breech report, be it written or be it verbal.
Let me say that my reason for suggesting the return of the former Prime Minister of this country to head a committee or commission to look into aircraft production in Canada was to assure the people of this dominion that there would be placed at the head of an investigation of our aircraft situation a man whose patriotism will never be doubted, a man whose industry and capabilities have meant so much in the past to this dominion.
We have business men in Canada to-day who are devoting their best talents to assisting this country at this time. I am not one of those who cast ridicule on men who are serving this country for one dollar a year. They are men whose aim is to contribute something to our war effort at this time, and I think one of the finest examples is Mr. H. R. MacMillan, chairman of the war-time requirements board, who in a speech delivered the other day in Vancouver epitomized the situation as he saw it as a result of the experience he had had. This is what he said in part:
In this case the balance sheet of Canada is the war. Nothing else matters. If we find that our capacity for making an effective war performance-say in the supply of ships and guns and aircraft and munitions-is defective, then it should be our duty to make the needed change without delay, and we should make it with one single motive, to increase the efficiency of our war effort.
Having regard to what has taken place and the objections that have been made by business men who have assumed positions of responsibility, naturally the question suggests
itself to all of us: Are the efforts of these business men being emasculated by controls exercised by government officials?
What of the aircraft situation? I have indicated the views of the Prime Minister and of Mr. Churchill on the importance of air power. Is the aircraft production situation in Canada to-day what it should be? The Minister of Munitions and Supply himself admitted that it was not, and he was quite frank in that regard. We have the right to know what the situation is. We have a responsibility not to sit by in silence and condone the failure of the government to organize properly the aircraft industry of this country.
Take the other side of the picture. What is the position in the United States of America? William Knudsen was appointed to take charge of aircraft production. What has happened? In December, 1940, it was expected that only 700 planes would be produced; the production was 799. In January, 1941, that production had increased to 1,306 planes, and it is ever on the increase, because the government of the United States realizes that only through an ever-accelerated aircraft production can the United States properly defend herself and assist this empire.
What of the situation in so far as Federal Aircraft Limited is concerned? The minister has stated that it was organized by the government to assure the production of fuselages for twin-engined Anson bombers, and to coordinate the industry throughout the dominion. It has failed to date. I say that, not in an attitude of gloating over that failure. The minister was optimistic last July when he spoke in this house, but he did not tell us it was optimism; at that time he indicated that the situation was such, with the organization of this particular corporation, that all would be well. These are his words on July 30, 1940, as reported in Hansard of that date at page 2116:
Early in 1941, we expect to have a production of 360 planes per month, or about 12 planes per day, Sundays and holidays included, on the basis of production now arranged for.
Those were his words. Production was arranged for; the expectation was placed before the house. Then he went on to say this:
In order to coordinate the work of these nine firms-
That is, those who were producing aircraft.
*-and to ensure a supply of raw materials, engines and instruments, as required, a wholly

War Appropriation Bill

Sovernment-owned company, Federal Aircraft limited, has been formed to take over the responsibility of the government for the production of aircraft of this type. It is anticipated that Canadian production of Ansons will commence before the end of this year.
That was the promise. The performance is that the promise is being carried into effect only in a very small measure. Why, even in November last, the minister asserted that all was well. According to Hansard, page 263 on November 20, he said this:
With regard to aircraft production, our aircraft industry is expanding rapidly and is producing planes to meet the requirements of the joint air training plan, and is also building operational aeroplanes for Great Britain and Canada. The output of planes is expanding each week in this new Canadian industry.
And then, a little further down:
The industry is in process of being reorganized on a production line basis.
That was the interim report. To-day the admission is that we are not producing sufficient planes for training purposes in Canada, and that it has become necessary to import such from the United' States.
What does Mr. MacMillan say in his report? His report on this matter appears on page 7 of the appendix to the Votes and Proceedings of February 27:
(L) Aircraft:
(1) (a) Anson's-Production might not start until after July, 1941, and might reach only 200 to 300 in 1941-
Compare that with the promise, the expectation in July, 1940. Mr. MacMillan continues:

but if carefully reorganized at several key points, and if time lost by failure of subcontractors can be recaptured, 1941 production might be doubled-
And so on. I ask the minister when he replies to tell the committee whether the "careful reorganization at several key points" has been proceeded with; if so, what was the nature of the reorganization, and1 what were the key points? Second, who are these subcontractors w'lio are to-day retarding the aircraft production of this dominion? I further ask him this, what reorganization is taking place to enable these qualified promises of production to become actualities? What assurance has parliament and this country that the record of failure established since the set-up of Federal Aircraft Limited, six months ago, will prove a foundation for success in the next six months?

I now refer the committee to an interview given by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, as reported in the Windsor Daily Star of February 1, 1941.

I now ask the minister to tell the committee whether the matter is still being considered, whether the continuation or discontinuance of this particular corporation is now being considered, or whether a final decision has been arrived at. I refer further to a statement that the minister made on his return from overseas, as reported in the press:
Federal Aircraft is in no worse shape than the rest of the aircraft industry in Canada.
Was that statement made as an excuse or as an indictment, because, when I read Mr. MacMillan's report, I find that the Noorduyn company, the Fleet, and the de Havilland are all on a smooth running basis and that their orders are being completed. They are commended for their efficiency?

The minister gave to the house before, in July and November, information that has not been justified by subsequent events, and we accepted those statements then. We are asking to-day to be assured that in the coming months the promises and the expectations of to-day will be the realization of to-morrow There were delays from July until now, delays until the 1st of July, 1941. The people of the country have a right to demand that these delays shall no longer be tolerated. If these machines are not turned out as they should-and the minister has been frank in that regard in saying that they have not been-then what the committee and the country want to know is, what changes will be effected that will ensure that such a condition shall not continue until the march by Hitler against the British empire commences?
The minister says that, because of the fact that we are able to secure supplies from the United States of America, our air training plan is not suffering. Yes. But if, perchance, that country went to war and it became necessary, 14873-834
in consequence, to assure a supply of these training planes for the United States, where would this nation be?
The MacMillan report says that the subcontractors have been to blame. Who they are we do not know; where they are we do not know. The committee wants to know, too, why it was that Federal Aircraft, set up as a designing corporation, went into private manufacture and acquired premises for factory purposes in the city of Montreal within the last few months. Who made the decision to alter the set-up of Federal Aircraft in that regard? Was it the company, or was it the minister himself? The minister has made the statement that all the plants in Canada are operating to capacity, and his explanation for delays is the fact that the industry is a new one and that it is not properly developed. I ask him, then, why it is that the de Havilland Corporation to-day is finding it necessary to reduce its shifts and hours. I ask why the Cub Aircraft Corporation in Hamilton, Ontario, which I am informed is able to produce Avro parts, is not being utilized. I ask why National Steel Car at Malton is not being operated to full capacity. Is it the subcontractors? Have they fallen down? If they have-and the evidence seems clear that they have-then I suggest to the minister that under the powers contained in the National Resources Mobilization Act the government act now and take over these corporations that are delinquent. Last June this legislation, the National Resources Mobilization Act, was put through the house, and we were told that it was necessary to ensure its early passage so that something could be done without delay. Here are the powers:
Subject to the provisions of section three hereof, the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of His Majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the war, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
The power is there. It was not put there for no purpose. It has not yet been used.

There were certain suggestions that I placed before the house the other day. In addition to those, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance as well as the Minister of Munitions and Supply to inform the committee whether a decision has been arrived at on the part of the government that the major portion of Canada's war effort should be restricted to the army or to the air force, because I notice that during the year ending January 31 some 3141,000,000 more was expended upon the army, upon the militia, than upon the air force. Yet we have been given to understand from time to time that aircraft production, personnel, et cetera, were considered one of the most important contributions that Canada could make.
With regard to Federal Aircraft, I would ask him to advise whether in his opinion its failure has been due in part to divided control. In England the government has set up no such corporation. Their efforts have won the admiration of the world. Each service is under the direct responsibility and supervision of a minister, aircraft production being under Lord Beaverbrook who is a member of the war cabinet and makes his report direct to parliament.
There is another phase I wish to take up, with a view to suggesting to the government that efforts be made and sanctions be adopted with a view to assuring that maximum efficiency shall characterize the expenditure of the moneys that are to-day being raised by both loan and taxation. The committee on war expenditures that was set up in Great

War Appropriation Bill
Britain studied this question at great length and came to conclusions that might very well be adopted by this parliament. I am not going into the matter in detail, except to refer to one recommendation that was made:
Your committee desire to record their emphatic opinion that no industry should be exempt from obligation to submit its costs to investigation by government accountants for the purpose of determining the prices to be paid under non-competitive contracts with government departments together with more supervision of costs where contracts are let on a cost-plus basis.
I am suggesting the adoption of a like principle for the consideration of the minister, in order to allay any suggestion of suspicion or concern in this country that will in any way undermine our war effort, because uncertainty and fear and suspicion will breed apathy in this nation and will result in a slackening of our war effort.

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER: Mr. Chairman, when the committee took recess I was dealing with the recommendation of the committee in the United Kingdom. I now pass on to another phase, and suggest that the government use the national registration to secure the labour categories which in course of time may become scarce, particularly with a view to ensuring that all technical men shall be mobilized in the service of the state.
I,	too, add my plea to that made by other hon. members that more effective use be made of smaller plants located throughout the dominion. I am more than pleased with the action of the government, taken with a view to securing stricter control of expenditures and to make possible the recommending of economies, in setting up the committee on war expenditures.
I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) state yesterday, if I understood him correctly, that so far as he was concerned the government was not going to demand that the committee sit in secret. In my opinion the only occasions upon which it should hold secret meetings would be those when the national safety might be jeopardized. I believe, if the meetings throughout are held in secret, suspicion will be aroused in the minds of some people that politics are being played. On the other hand if, for the most part, the sessions of the committee are held openly, the people of Canada will be able to judge as to what members of the committee
are endeavouring in any way to play politics, whether they be on the side of the government or of the opposition.
There must be stricter control of expenditures; the people have asked for it. I was pleased with the attitude displayed by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Abbott) and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson). Their attitude was that taken by this party, namely, that it will be our desire to enter the committee in a sincere spirit of patriotism. We will approach the work, not with a desire to search out picayune faults, but with an honest desire to help the war effort, and to make recommendations, general as they must be, to speed up the tempo of the war effort. We will endeavour to ascertain what, if anything, is holding up the production of munitions, if indeed there is such a hold-up; and, in particular, we will inquire into the hold-up in aircraft production and have an opportunity to suggest remedies.
The people, however, must not expect too much from the committee. If we are to sit until the end of the session, a matter of only two months and a half, at the outside, in view of the fact that to this date 85,000 contracts have been awarded and 1,500 new contracts are being awarded each week, it must be realized that all the committee can do is to generalize. It will not and cannot, as I conceive the situation to be, enter into consideration of individual contracts.
The attitude of Conservative members on the committee, as it has been in the house, will be to subordinate party interests to the public good, just as the blueprint of this party since the outbreak of the war has been to couple fair criticism with honest cooperation with the government in a national war effort.	[DOT]
In conclusion, I would say that, before this debate is concluded, we want action with regard to the matter of aircraft production. The country must be assured that the failures of the past will be rectified. It must be assured that anyone who to-day is hampering production in any of the departments, either through inefficiency or negligence, must go. After eighteen months of war, the period of trial and error should be over. We do not wish to criticize only for the sake of advancing arguments to injure the government. Far be it from us to take that attitude,-although the government has shown signs of being allergic to all types of criticism. Our attitude is that aircraft production must be speeded up. In this life and death struggle there will be no second chance for our empire. Excuses for non-production of aeroplanes or other munitions of war will avail nothing when the test with Hitler arises.
War Appropriation Bill

To-day people are making demands. They are asking us-and that is why we are here- to get assurance that the maximum war effort of which this country is capable shall be given. They are asking for a maximum, measured not in terms of amounts but rather in amounts coupled with effectiveness and efficiency. The people of Canada want to help. They want the facts. They are prepared to face those facts, and if mistakes have been made they want to know that those mistakes have not been and will not be condoned.
Let us all in a spirit of cooperation and calm deliberation meet this challenge to our very liberties and our lives; and when a course is decided upon or when changes must be made in the interests of the safety of the state, let us proceed to carry out those plans ruthlessly and with determination.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped not to say anything in this debate, because I know the minister is quite capable of taking care of himself. I would, however, be derelict in my duty if I did not say that we are thankful to the Almighty that he is here tonight and is able to come bubbling up over the top of all this fighting just as safely as he did) when that boat was sunk on the other side of the Atlantic. I feel it is the duty of hon. members to show up any weak spots, but when the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) was dealing with the aircraft industry I was sorry that he stopped short o'f Fort William.
Fort William is alive. A writer in a magazine stated that no Hurricanes were being made in Canada, but Hurricanes are being made at Fort William. Fort William is in Canada; therefore the logical conclusion is that they are being made in Canada. Some have said that no Hurricanes are being made, that they are just being assembled. We admit that the engines come from the other side; but if hon. members could see, as I have seen, the piles of raw material, of long pipes, of large sheets of metal, all of which are to be cut and filed into shape and fitted to the proper spot on the plane, they would realize that a great deal is being done there. When it is said that no Hurricanes are being made in Canada, they should think of Fort William. I know that all planes made in Fort William or any other place in Canada are made either for the dominion government or for overseas under the control of the dominion government. It is impossible for a plane to be shipped out of Canada without the authority of the government of Canada through the Department of External Affairs.
The factory at Fort William is increasing its production all the time. It is expected that it will be producing twenty-five or more

planes a week. Judging from the present results, I know the number will be more. For the week ending February 8, they produced seven planes, or one a day; for the. week ending February 15, they produced fourteen; for the week ending February 22, they produced thirteen and for the week ending March 1, they produced fifteen. The small production in the first week of February was due to a shortage of material. Much of this material was being procured from Great Britain and perhaps Germany was able to prevent some of this from reaching Canada. The minister, however, made some trips to the United' States, and he has found a way for us to get engines and other material. I think we have a right to be grateful for that.
I should like to say a word about the management. The management of this aeroplane factory at Fort William is as efficient as the management of any other concern in Canada. Generally speaking, the foremen and inspectors are locally trained, although there are some exceptions. Young men who went to school in Fort William and Port Arthur were taken on and trained in the making of an obsolete plane called the Grumman. At that time this plant could not obtain permission to make a more up-to-date or modem plane. One of these young men is the general foreman, and I would say that there is no better man in Canada. He has considerable sense because when he found a young lady he liked, he had a member of this house help him tie the knot.

All I know is that when the Canadian Car wanted to send planes out of Canada, they had to get the permission of the former Minister of National Defence, the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). I do not think there is anything that goes out of Canada to Great Britain, or even out of the United States to

War Appropriation Bill
Great Britain which is not known to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and Mr. Purvis.
I was speaking of the staff when I was interrupted. The staff is well balanced because there are about 500 girls working in the plant. That shows that in this plant there is the making of a future great industry which will go far beyond its present capacity. Then, again, this plant is staffed by men and women who honour the right of men to organize. They have one of the best trades unions at the head of the lakes, one which is second to none in Canada. They had a terrific job organizing this union because employment increased so rapidly. I should like to pay my tribute to the trades union executive. These men have the milk of human kindness in their hearts. When a man passes on or someone suffering from sickness must go away for treatment, they pay the bills. I do not know of any other organization in Canada which does that sort of thing.
This organization has banded together and has donated one and perhaps two Hurricanes. The Montreal plant is donating the material and the men and women at Fort William are giving two days' pay, which ranges from about $8 up. These Hurricanes will not cost the Canadian or the British government one cent, and we hope the British government will accept them, as I think they will, in the spirit in which they are given. There is another thing about this splendid plant at Fort William which I should like to mention. "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy." That proverb lives because it is true. The men of this plant organized their athletics with the same energy that they give to their jobs. Last summer they won the hard-ball championship of the Thunder Bay district and they played so well that the big league scouts were up there looking for talent for the coming season.
They entered a team in the hockey league this winter. Against keen competition they have topped the league. They are ready to go through a stone wall to secure a goal or make a home run. They are putting into their games the same energy as they put into their work. I ask the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) to note this. If all other organizations are like this one, there is nothing to worry about. Then the production will be like that wheat which they used to raise in Manitoba in the early days, and sometimes yet, known as No. 1 hard.
There has been no sabotage in this plant because the man in charge of maintenance showed great sense by appointing a real Irishman as a policeman in charge of the guard.
They know they are being taken care of. This all-round industry is very sensitive, and so am I when members in this house say that it is not functioning with efficiency. It is functioning far better than I ever expected it would function, and I visit the plant regularly. If all war industry in Canada were functioning as efficiently as this one plant, I am sure that Hitler would soon find himself in the place where he hoped to send the Minister of Munitions and Supply when his boat was torpedoed.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Lake Centre upon one suggestion that he has made. He thought it would be a good thing to invite the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett to come back to Canada. I am sure that if he came back and spent six months under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), he would never sit among my hon. friends to my left on this side of the house but would blossom out as a real Liberal so that wherever he might be he would have honest Liberal action.
There is one thing more I should like to say about the plant at Fort William. I believe that it will lead the rest of Canada, just as it is leading it now in production, in efficiency, in harmony among the workers, and in kindness and courtesy between the management and the staff, and I resent anybody in this house saying one word against the minister who fathers an organization of that kind. He has given gladly of his time. I have invited him out of the house on several occasions to meet the executive of the Canadian Car, and he has always surprised me by accepting the invitation. Sometimes we would meet in room 16 and sometimes upstairs, and the knowledge he had of aeroplanes and the aeroplane industry in those early days was a revelation to me. He showed the executive of the Canadian Car that he knew far more than they did, and I gladly pay my tribute to the minister. I get a little bit hot when anybody blames him for insufficiency or Shortcomings. He has always been honest and fair and has conducted his department in such a way that the government and the people of this country can take off their hats and say: "Thank God he is living."

Mr. Chairman, I am
sure that we all feel refreshed by the address of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), but I wish he had told us just where he thinks the minister would have gone had Hitler succeeded in sending him on his way. For fear there may be any misapprehension as to the region the hon. member had in mind, I am sure that he meant the minister would have gone to heaven.
War Appropriation Bill

In view of the bitterness of the remarks of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) when he spoke earlier in this debate and the bitterness of the Prime Minister's remarks in reference to anyone who might offer any suggestion that might be construed as criticism, I hardly know how far I should go. However, I was sent here to speak on behalf of my constituents and I am going to present my arguments as I see fit. But, before doing so, I should like to repeat to the minister, for whom I have a warm feeling as one business man for another, a verse that I quoted once for the benefit of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) when in former years he would get hot under the collar and say something that perhaps he did not intend. I must say that he has greatly improved since he took to heart this ancient verse which I am now going to quote for the Minister of Munitions and Supply, with the hope that he, too, will not get so hot under the collar from now on, because, after all, when a man gets heated he loses control of himself.
Here is an ancient Brahmin proverb which I found in a very old book. It reads like this:
Proceed not to speak or act, before thou hast weighed thy words, and examined the tendency of every step thou shalt take: so shall disgrace fly far from thee, and in thy house shame shall be a stranger; repentance shall not visit thee, nor sorrow dwell upon thy cheek.
From what the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said this afternoon, it would appear that the minister, being heated perhaps, has on one or two occasions given different answers to the same question, but if he keeps before him the verse I have just quoted I hope he will be able to control himself from now on.
For my part, I admit that every member of this house is just as sincere as I am in trying to plan to win this war. I do not think there is in this house any man or woman either who is anything but sincere in doing what he or she can to win the war. So I grant all sincerity to the minister in what he has done.
At the same time I hope that the minister and the Prime Minister will admit that the press is also sincere. I cannot for the life of me understand why any bitter words should be heaped upon the press. They have a number of highly paid men on their staffs, although not anything like as highly paid as they should be. To be a successful journalist a man must have a love of writing and digging, and they never get paid for that. But they do write and dig, and give advice; and whenever I have seen in the press what might in some quarters be interpreted as criticism of 
the efforts of the minister or of the government, I take it that it was advice honestly given to urge the government towards further improvement. I am quite satisfied that the journalists and the press of this country are as sincere as any of us in this house in our desire to win the war. Then why criticize them bitterly as they were criticized earlier in this debate for what they wrote for the benefit of this dominion?
Similarly I believe that every member of this house is sincere in what he says. We may not agree, but we are all sincere in what we have said.
I should like now to refer to a few of these press articles to see if they are guilty of the insincerity that was attributed to them earlier in this debate. On February 5-that was pretty early, just about the commencement of criticism of a strong nature-there appeared in the Toronto Telegram an editorial entitled:
Fumbling on vital matters painfully apparent at Ottawa.
The minister and the Prime Minister may have been annoyed at the heading of that editorial, but it is absolutely true. The editorial reads:
Critics of the compulsory thirty-day military camps who held that these brief periods of training were useless in making soldiers out of civilians, and therefore a waste of money, find confirmation for their opinions in the announcement by Prime Minister King that draftees will now be given a minimum of four months' instruction.
The editorial goes on to quote the reason which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) gave for the thirty-day training plan, namely, that so many more men could be trained. Further on, it refers to the fact that the longer period will ensure that the men will be much better trained, and that is admitted by the government. Therefore the press were not in any error in saying that. They were right, too, in saying there was fumbling, because there certainly was. Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that we often fly off with no sound ground for doing so.
I remember what the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) said about the manufacturers, that if they were not big enough to do such and such and let their men get away for the thirty days training, they were not big enough to run industries, or words to that effect. Later on, however, the Prime Minister approved an extension of time so that industry would not be injured in that way by the thirty-day training plan. The press was not wrong in that instance.

No, I know the minister did not. I come to the Telegram of February 6. It says:
Lack of competent direction is paralyzing Canada's war effort.
Perhaps the government and the minister were annoyed at that.
Following the recent statements of air minister Power and supply minister Howe the government can no longer cloak the fact that its aeroplane production programme is in a terrible tangle.
The editorial makes reference to the air minister having said that the necessity to use three planes in training where he should have had four, was not his fault. But, being a really courteous minister, he did not care to elaborate on that. In fact, if I might digress for a moment, I regard our air minister as one of the best members of the cabinet. He has backbone, and I admire a man with backbone.
Here is another editorial, written in Ottawa by the editor of the Journal and commented upon in the Globe of February 6, entitled "The Part Canada Plays". Perhaps the minister, or the government, or both, might be annoyed by the tenor of the editorial. A comparison is there made between the results of the programmes in Australia and in Canada. The Australian programme does show up pretty satisfactorily. I am not going to denounce or belittle Canada's war effort, but it could be better. I have criticized what has been done, but I am not going to decry Canadians.
The next item is one of February 7 in the Globe, entitled "King Ministry Misled Public, Hepburn Says". The minister and hon. members have read what Premier Hepburn said about the government's war effort, and there is no reason why the press should be denounced because of what the premier of Ontario said.
The Montreal Gazette had an article on February 17 entitled, "Equipment Lack Bars Volunteers", and quotes the Minister of National War Services as having said this:
Canada has not been able to use all those who have volunteered for military service since the beginning of the war "because we haven't had the equipment."
That is what the rest of us say; that is what the press says; and therefore there is no reason why either an individual or a journal should be denounced for that.
Then, on February 22, the Financial Post, under the heading "Claims Federal Aircraft Suffers Basic Weakness", says this:
Failure of Federal Aircraft, Limited, to maintain its production schedule is not the only reason why the company should be condemned to the "scrap heap" in the view of Canadian Aviation, recognized authority on aircraft in Canada.
And so on; one article after another. I have read many of them, and I cannot see any reason whatever for heat on the part of the minister or the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister was particularly bitter the other evening when he denounced criticism.

I want to get right down to fundamentals in one matter in particular, and that is, who called the conference which met in Ottawa at the end of December or early in January?
Mr. LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency): Nobody knows.

My leader, in making his address, did try to ascertain exactly who called the conference. He said this, as reported in Hansard, page 1060.
I asked whether early in the year he did not request an opportunity to discuss aeroplane production problems with manufacturers interested in Anson bombers.
The minister of munitions was away. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), who was acting Minister of Munitions and Supply at the time of the conference, replied:
In answer to my hon. friend's question, there was a discussion between the manufacturers of component parts of Avro-Anson bombers, on the one hand, and myself on the other. Whether I requested it or they requested it I am not sure. They came to Ottawa and requested to see me and I spent an hour or two with them.
To me, who called the conference is an important matter, because that is the beginning of the so-called criticism, or of what resulted in the so-called criticism. It i3 a fact that the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, then acting Minister of Munitions and Supply, did invite the manufacturers here to Ottawa. There is no question about it.

He requested them to come to Ottawa-and rightly, in my judgment. When I got full confirmation of that I said to myself, "the minister of naval services must be a business man, because that is just what a business man would do." Not knowing, perhaps, much, if anything, about aeroplane production, what would a man do who really wished to inquire? He would send for the men who knew. After having a discussion with them, he asked them to send a report, which they did. I am not going to deal with the report particularly; it was dealt with fully by the hon. member for Lake Centre. But one of the clauses asked for the dissolution of Federal Aircraft. That is very plain. After reading the report and observing that the principal request was for the dissolution of Federal Aircraft, the acting minister likely concluded, in my judgment quite rightly, "Now this is a big matter; I will wait until the minister comes home; he will soon be here."
When the minister came home and had the report put before him, he exhibited immediately, I think, a little bit of heat, for the letter which he wrote to the aircraft manufacturers is not in my judgment the most courteous letter that could have been written. Probably he was hurt at the request to dissolve Federal Aircraft. I would not have acted in that way. I myself was employed in big business for a quarter of a century-a business employing well on to a thousand men-

speechtext:
The minister wrote, on January 31:
On my return from the United Kingdom my attention has been called to the document signed by yourself and several others. . . .
Recommendations signed by six firms with some experience in the manufacture of aircraft-
They are the only people in Canada who had any experience. They are all big manufacturers.
-or components must, of course, receive careful consideration.
Then he asked questions, of which No. 3 is:
As one of the contractors holding a subcontract for this production, what guarantee can you and your group give as to the date when substantial deliveries of Anson planes will be made, provided your recommendations are adopted?
What would I have done? I would have sent for the manufacturers and talked to them across the desk as big men. The minister himself is a big man. He was a business man building big things such as docks, elevators harbours and so on in his time, and that is what he would have done in his own business. It is also what he should have done in this instance. He should have sent for these men and said, "Let us talk over the table so that I can get your views. I am as anxious as you are to produce aeroplanes in large numbers to win this war".
The first step was the calling of a conference; the second step was asking for the report, and the third step was the return home of the minister and the writing of the letter to the manufacturers.
I should like to go back to the minister's own statements. They were given this afternoon, but it will not hurt to repeat them now. They will be found at page 263 of Hansard of November 20. The minister said:
The industry is in process of being reorganized on a production line basis. Canada is now building complete aeroplanes except for the engines, and, for the present, engines are being purchased either in the United States or in Great Britain. Production covers practically every type of training plane in use in Canada and several types of operational planes.
From that I would gather that at the time that statement was made on November 20 last, production was pretty well under way, but earlier, in the month of July, the minister had made this statement. On July 30 he said:
Federal Aircraft Limited has been formed to take over the responsibility of the government for the production of aircraft of this type. It is anticipated that Canadian production of Ansons will commence before the end of the year.

War Appropriation Bill
It is almost eight months since that statement was made, and yet Ansons are not being produced in Canada. There is one plane that is being tested and examined, and I presume that in due course the engineers in charge of that plane will arrive at a conclusion as to how the plane should be finally constructed.
Recently the minister said that it would be next April or May before Ansons would be ready to fly, but the MacMillan report, referred to earlier to-day, staves off the time until next July or August; and it is still problematical. The question is, exactly when are these planes going to be constructed? Apparently they are very necessary for training. They are good bombers and good fighters, and in my judgment they should have been turned out before this.
Something was said to-day about the cutting down of hours in these plants. The reason why hours are being cut down is, as I understand, the shortage of skilled mechanics in Canada. The shifts have been reduced from three to two, two ten-hour shifts. I would point out that trained, skilled mechanics cannot be turned out in two or three months. Any business man knows that. An executive is not trained in two or three months, and therefore, by reducing the shifts, they are able to cut down the demand for such men. I am not sure that they will not produce as much, because where a plant operates in three shifts the machines do not go on immediately on each eight-hour schedule. It takes some time for one shift to step out and the other to come in.
In my opinion the government deserves some censure or blame for the fact that in Canada there has been a shortage of skilled mechanics and trained executives to operate machine plants. I remember, after I returned from England in 1937, I told the government in 1938, in the course of the session that yeaT, that, according to the figures I had obtained from the immigration department in England, Canada had already lost from 25,000 to
30,000	skilled mechanics. I warned the government on that occasion that the time would come when those mechanics would be required here. I say, therefore, that the government deserves some censure for the fact that all those skilled mechanics left the country. That was a large number of skilled men to leave this dominion.
I also warned the government that it was necessary for us to get into aeroplane production. I will not read from Hansard what I said at that time, but in 1937 I had made a close inquiry into aeroplane production in continental Europe, particularly in Germany, and during the course of the debates that took place then-the present Minister of
Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) was Minister of National Defence at the time-I strongly recommended that Canada get into aeroplane production; because, from my observations in Germany, I was of opinion that everybody would fly-well, not everybody; that is an exaggeration. Certainly, however, there were very large numbers of aviators passing through the stations in Berlin. I sat in one of the stations there for hours and mentally counted aviators getting on and off trains, and I estimated that in that one station there were about 1,500 men that I observed. There are twelve stations in Berlin and I remember calculating at the time, multiplying 1,500 by twelve, that Germany when she was ready would fight in the air, because there were thus probably 18,000 aviators in Berlin alone. In view of this I warned the government that they should get into aeroplane production.
The same with regard to machine tools. Look at the trouble we are in to-day in this respect. That is one of the troubles in connection with the aeroplane business. I am told on good authority that a large number of machine tools were purchased in Chicago, by the machine controller I presume, and that a goodly number of machines are unsatisfactory for the work for which they were acquired-shapers, planers, slotters, drills and so forth. We are partly to blame for that. After I returned from my last visit to Britain, I made a statement in this house that I had met different manufacturers in England who were ready to build branch plants in this country. I was more or less laughed at for making that statement, but no less a man than the Minister of Munitions and Supply himself gave out a statement that plants would move to Canada, as can be verified by reference to an article headed "Howe Reports British Firms to Move Here." I felt at the time that Canada should be the arsenal and manufacturing plant for Great Britain if at all possible, if and when war broke out.

speechtext: What year was that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

That was in 1938. I made a statement to the house. In the opinion of anyone travelling through Great Britain as I did, surveying factories by the dozen, large factories, some with as high as 35,000 to 40,000 men, and additions being made, it would have been only sound business on Canada's part to induce some of those new branch plants to come here, because those large bombs would blow some of those plants that I have in mind, off the map. If we had those plants in Canada
War Appropriation Bill

now, we would be in much better shape to produce aeroplanes and other equipment required to win this war.
The minister said, I believe a year ago more or less, that it would take about eighteen months to build an aeroplane engine plant in Canada. Well, they built them in Australia; they manufacture their engines in Australia to-day; in fact, they manufacture everything pertaining to aeroplanes except magnetos and carburetors.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They are not manufacturing every kind of engine there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
They are exporting planes from Australia, and their Wirraway is an extremely fine aeroplane. In an editorial in the Citizen of March 4, it is stated:
Aircraft engines have been imported from the United States to Australia, but the Commonwealth Air Corporation last December celebrated the delivery of its 200th Wirraway war plane entirely designed and manufactured in Australia, with the exception of magnetos and carburetors.
We can do the same thing in Canada. No country in the world has better mechanics than Canada. I say, go to it and try to develop an engine manufacturing plant in Canada, because this war will last more than another eighteen months; and if we have another eighteen months of slaughter in Europe, it may be necessary to manufacture thousands of engines as well as entire planes in Canada.
This is the criticism I would offer to the minister as one business man to another. When it became necessary to develop the aircraft business and build up the manufacture of aeroplanes, instead of setting up the Federal Aircraft corporation with some very good men -I have nothing but good to say about any of them, but what would the minister 'have done had it been a question of building grain elevators and docks? He would certainly have surrounded himself with men who knew something about the erection of elevators and docks. What would I have done if it were a case of the manufacture of boilers and radiators? I would have surrounded myself with men who knew something about them, and about the rolling of steel and the melting of iron.
The same thing should have been done with regard to aircraft. I would have gone to one of these big aeroplane companies and said, "You do all the pilot work for the manufacture of the Anson plane in your plant." In that way only one group of technicians and executives would be used to develop all that is required to make an Anson plane, whereas if three or four different plants, including Federal,

which is a small business, were all engaged, that would increase the number of executives and technicians and experts required. It strikes me as a much better thing to use one of the big plants, any one of them, to develop and complete all that is required to produce the Anson and then say to all the other companies "There, gentlemen, there are the designs and the tools; there are all the particulars in connection with the manufacture of this type of plane; now go to it." One plant would have been the pilot plant and all would do the manufacturing.
I was interested to read this morning about the German bombers now arriving on the borders of Greece. The article said that the fourth German squadron, which is now on the borders of Greece, has apparently about seventeen hundred planes and bombers. That bears out what I saw in Germany. I looked to the future with a good deal of fear-temporary fear-I have no doubt we shall win when we once get organized; we have always won before and we will this time. But at the moment, if the fourth bomber squadron has 1,700 planes, it bears out what I saw in Germany, that there are many thousands of them. We must do the same thing here.
If I were the minister, and I thought for one moment that by calling in the present aeroplane builders or anyone else who could give advice, a better way could be found, I would forget all I had done, if by doing so I could improve for the future. It is absolutely necessary to forget all bitterness or recrimination; that is of no value; it is all water gone under the mill. What we must do now is all to get together with the best we have in the country and produce the most we can to win this war, all- of us; for, if we lose, we all go down. That is my parting word.
I have the best of feeling towards the minister. As one business man to another I say: I know your problems; I have been through them; all big business has its problems, and many times I have had to retrace my steps, wash out everything that was behind and commence over again. Many times we have spent money in making preparations that we thought were right, have spent a hundred thousand dollars, perhaps more, found we were wrong, washed it out and started over again, and we finally won. Some people may have lost confidence in the minister. I have not; I feel sorry for him. I say to myself, to whom in the cabinet can he go for advice?
