The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley).

War Appropriation Bill

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The Minister of Finance is a financial man and a bright lawyer from Nova Scotia, but the minister wants business advice, technical advice, advice from capable, brilliant manufacturers who have had many years of experience. They do not grow like mushrooms, it takes years and years to develop a capable administrator. I have nothing but the best to say about the cabinet. There has been a good deal of talk about changing the government; that is all past as far as I am concerned; but if the government is to be improved, I should say there should be taken into it some big business executives upon whom the minister could call.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What about labour?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And labour too, a good labour man, a real labour man, an experienced man who perhaps has worked from the bottom to the top. I would trust him; I would not seek advice from a man who had had no executive experience. But what the minister wants is help; he is carrying too big a load to do it alone. As an hon. member said, I, too, thank God the minister came back safely, because he is a big man-yes, I will say this further; I believe it was an act of Divine Providence that he was saved though others were taken; his ability and experience were required here. I am a great believer in God Almighty and His divine direction.
I say to the minister: Retrace your steps. These big executives have said, dismiss Federal Aircraft. That is no criticism of Federal Aircraft; they are good men; in their own line they may be all right. But the manufacture of aeroplanes is a highly specialized business. We must win the war, and if I were the minister I would set an objective of 50,000 planes. If I were Minister of National Defence for Air, or whatever it is he is called-there are getting to be so many ministers I am getting mixed up, myself-I would set an objective of 50,000 aviators and bombers. I would fill the skies over Germany with bombers. There are no better aviators in the world than the Canadians. The Australians are good, and so are the New Zealanders. But none are better than the Canadians. It may be that they have not yet had an opportunity to show what they can do. But I would blacken the sun out over Germany with aeroplanes!
But to do that you have to build them in Canada. Start your engine plant. Even if it takes eighteen months to build it, you can do it. I know you can. Build the engines. I know we are told there would have to be several kinds. No matter how many kinds are needed, let us remember that this is an
all-out war. We have to stake all! We have to win! If it requires planes and plants and executives and men and munitions, the minister can do it. But retrace your steps. Let him surround himself with big, successful, executive men, who will back him up when he encounters difficulties, and then manufacture, manufacture, manufacture more planes 1

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre in his views respecting dollar-a-year men. I find it difficult to follow the hon. member for Davenport. Whether or not he was trying to criticize the government, I was unable to say. But I think he was offering the same old criticism we have heard day after day from the official opposition.
The war appropriation bill now before the committee of the whole contains figures so enormous that sometimes one is likely to conclude that such figures are beyond the human resources of this nation. In the early days of this debate the hon. member for Trinity explained forcefully how these figures mean very little. He pointed out that, after all, only goods and services really matter, and that it is goods and services which constitute the real wealth of this nation.
The staggering amount mentioned in the bill will be accepted by the House of Commons and by the Canadian people, and still more staggering amounts will, in years to come, be accepted by the house and by the Canadian people, because as many hon. members have said, we are in this war to defend that very freedom which was handed down to us by our forefathers. It is difficult, of course, for many people living in the quiet countrysides of western Canada and on the peaceful prairie lands to think that this dominion would ever see the ravages of war. We know that things have happened in other countries, and it is not beyond the bounds of human possibility that such things may happen in our own country.
In discussing the few points which come to one's mind in connection with this appropriation bill I find it difficult to know, in these days of tragedy and tears, whether it is in the best interests of Canada to offer praise or criticism of the administration. After all, they do deserve a certain amount of praise. I do not for one minute believe there is one minister who is not doing everything within his power to make this war effort as efficient as possible. Constructive criticism has, however, been the very cornerstone of our parliamentary form of government.
There is one criticism I should like to reiterate, one which has been made in the
War Appropriation Bill

house before, and one which is heard to-day throughout the country, and that has to do with the status to which members of parliament have come in this house. Once upon a time a letter of recommendation from a member of parliament meant something. But to-day, to be recommended by a member of parliament, even for a country post office position, or as to fitness to receive foreign exchange, would immediately lead to the possibility of being turned down. It would be a handicap. The only thing a member can do is to recommend that the applicant go to some police officer or someone of that kind, because we realize that a member of parliament cannot give letters of recommendation to any of his constituents. Who should be more qualified than members of parliament, those who have been elected by the will of the people, to give letters of recommendation? Who should be more qualified than those who have been placed in positions of public responsibility, regardless of their party affiliations, to recommend residents of the districts in which they live?
During this debate there have been various types of criticism. I wish first of all to say that, although I may disagree with many of the policies of the present administration, I will never engage in any personal criticism of a particular minister. I believe attacks against the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) are completely unwarranted, because no man either in or out of this house has a more enviable reputation for honesty, ability and devotion to duty. The very fact that a suggestion was made that he should be leader of this country, irrespective of the political hook the opposition intended to place upon him, indicated the high regard in which he was held throughout the country. The opposition group would never have suggested his name, had his ability not been known throughout the length and breadth of the dominion.
Then, we remember the abuse which was heaped upon a great western Canadian newspaper, the Winnipeg Free Press. Throughout the years that paper has become almost the western farmers' Bible. It has attained that reputation over a long period of time, and it certainly deserves the position it holds. For a long time Doctor Dafoe was its guiding hand, a man who is recognized as a great journalist, probably the greatest Canada has ever produced. The breadth of his vision, the soundness of his background, his knowledge and his public-spirited Canadianism are known from ocean to ocean. The newspaper to a considerable extent has taken on the character of the man. Although it does speak its mind freely when it believes the party is wrong, or when it is misguided, it has been the bulwark of progressive thought throughout

the years on western Canada's plains. Although Clifford Sifton did break with Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the famous election campaign of 1911, the Winnipeg Free Press did not. It carried on its fight for lower tariffs and reciprocal trade relations with the United States. In that campaign the people who forsook Sir Wilfrid Laurier were his own French-Canadians, the nationalists from Quebec.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, there are so many high-ranking Tories in key positions in this country that the present opposition is able only to tap at any criticism it wants to make. It will never say anything about any departments of government. Every time we meet here they throw up their old smoke-screens asking for a union government or a national government, or for a change in the leadership. This is just a replica of the same old story that their former leader, the Hon. Doctor Manion, carried on throughout the length and breadth of Canada. But when the present Prime Minister asked him to name some of the men about whom the hon. member for Danforth has been talking, those great brains in the country, he was never able to name any.
The only person who has ever been named here was named, by the hon. member for Lake Centre. He mentioned that great man, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, and suggested that the Liberal government should return him to power, or return him to Canada. This was the man who in a peace-time crisis was discredited by the Canadian electors. The Conservatives virtually threw him overboard, and that is why he is not in this country.
I sometimes wonder whether it is going to be possible for us to continue on this nonpartisan government basis. When this part of the session opened, the Prime Minister pointed out that it was more than ever necessary that we steel our hearts and minds to the magnitude of the effort and the sacrifice that would be demanded of us over a considerable period of time. In special measure throughout the next few months the government, because of its party affiliations, will be faced with criticism which is not justified. This government has certainly divested itself of all partisanship, but it is difficult for the public mind to grasp that fact. As the gravity of the war situation grows more intense, it will not be difficult to see what may happen with a nonpartisan government. The war is bound to be long and we must do our utmost to promote the best war effort possible. Even though members of this administration may think they are doing everything possible, yet this may not be good enough, it may not be broad enough. It is either freedom for free

War Appropriation Bill
men, or medieval slavery. There is no inbetween measure; there is no half way measure in the new order that has been set up by the dictators of the totalitarian states.
It is our duty to eliminate from all branches of the service all intrigue and ineffectuality that are seething underneath. These are the things that interfere more than anything else with our war effort. Some of us wish to bring them into the open. If they are brought to the light of day, incompetency, inefficiency and unethical practices will not long remain. There is no use in protesting that they do not flourish and exist in certain places. Of course they do. One of the reasons for this is the fact that Tory magnates from all over Canada are being placed in high positions of authority. Then what do we find? They immediately surround themselves with their Tory heelers. Since the government became non-partisan, we have had grow up a system of bureaucratic patronage that is far more dangerous than any system under which a government appoints its own supporters.
A government must defend its actions in parliament. These dollar-a-year men do not have to stand up in this chamber to defend their actions. That is why none of them would go into the government or assume any position in parliament. They knew they would then have to stand up to defend themselves. At present they defend themselves behind their offices. One does not have to go far afield in this city of Ottawa to see them. They are all over the place and they are working to the detriment of the administration in power at this time. It is an extremely dangerous practice to appoint as controller of a commodity or industry a person who has a large stake in that particular industry. The natural human tendency is to use such control, which amounts almost to a dictatorship, for private interests. We can see many cases of this on all sides. Take this MacMillan affair. Mr. MacMillan should have given an explanation immediately to the press. But no; the people were kept in suspense.
Pick up almost any Ontario newspaper and you will find how the heads of these large organizations throughout this province are criticizing members of parliament or anyone else who offer any opposition by way of constructive criticism. I have looked a number of these men up and checked over the contracts they have. One that is in my mind at the moment is the Otis-Fensom Elevator company. The president of this company is Mr. W. D. Black, and this gentleman was
most severe in his criticism about those who had anything to say about the government. Here is what he said:
There is no evidence that a protracted campaign of minority criticism at the present time can contribute anything to our war effort. There is conclusive evidence that it can seriously impair it, by confusing and distracting the public, at a time when solidarity and a deep sense of common responsibility are absolutely indispensable.
I checked things over, and I found that this company had received capital assistance totalling $9,000,000 from this country and Great Britain. It is easy to understand why this gentleman can say that there should be no criticism. All of these chaps who have these large contracts are against criticism. That is one of the reasons why the Tory opposition dare not criticize these parties. I realize that in a war emergency an excellent case can be made out for increasing cabinet or executive authority. I am not saying that I do not approve that action in a crisis, but executive authority should be employed to fuse all the elements of the country into cooperative enterprise. When it simply becomes an appropriation of the functions of government by a few, then it takes on all the worst features of a dictatorship with little of the redeeming advantages. Democracy is a testament of man's faith in man, but I can find but little faith being placed in members of this house by the administration in the last few months. One member of the government who has taken this House of Commons more into his confidence than any other member of the government is the Minister of Agriculture and Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner). He has done this in connection with the national registration and again in connection with the national salvage campaign.
He has been criticized in both eastern and western Canada. In western Canada they say that he has not done enough for western agriculture, but he has been responsible for every progressive piece of legislation on behalf of agriculture that has been put upon our statute books, such as the acreage bonus, the minimum price of wheat and the active administration of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I disagreed with him in connection with the minimum price of wheat, because I thought the price of 70 cents a bushel was too low. He has not tried to wiggle out of facing the difficulties in which agriculture finds itself. He has met these questions face to face, whether in Saskatoon or in London, Ontario. Wherever he has been, he has made out a splendid case for himself. He has told
War Appropriation Bill

them straight from the shoulder what the situation was and has not tried to paint any glorious picture for agriculture. He has not advised people to go into the production of pork products or some other commodity, but has explained to them the situation as he saw it. When he returned from England he told the people the exact situation that had been presented to him by the British government. He told the people the details of the wheat situation that existed. He did not rise in his place in the house and advise the farmers of the country to go into the raising of this or that commodity.
The minister has been criticized by the industrialists of the east because he had the courage to rise in his place in this House of Commons and defend his leader when he was being attacked. It was being said that our leader was not a good war Prime Minister although he was all right in peace time. When the minister told the industrialists that the young men in their employ would have to take military training, he was taking the long view of this situation. I think in a year or so the minister will be vindicated. After all these guns are manufactured, there will have to be someone to shoot them. What will these particular factories do when the young men go into training? They will have to change their system and employ older men. That is exactly what the minister was advising them to do, and yet there was a storm of protest in the eastern press.
Everyone wishes to do his or her part in this great war effort. When the minister initiated this national salvage campaign he left it to the members of the House of Commons to do their part. Yet we have one hon. member rising in his place and using most unparliamentary terms when he said that we were supposed to collect bones and scrap-iron. It must be remembered that those particular commodities are made into explosives and guns which will be placed in the hands of our fighting forces. In 1920, Doctor Charles F. Horne, editor of The Great Events of the Great War said:
The war could no more have been avoided than an earthquake or any other cataclysm of nature's unknown forces. On the one side loomed the German character of strength and patience, of selfish caution in adversity and vain and reckless arrogance in power. On the other, glowed the sunlight of democratic civilization, which has taught all people to aspire to equality, and to prefer death to slavery Given these opposing forces, and their clash was inevitable. The marvel now is only that we were slow to see the ominous approach to the disaster.
"The war that shall end all war!" Has the human race passed through that stupendous final experience of the great tragedy, the terror 
and the splendour and despair of destruction and devotion? We may all hope so, but mere hope will do little to change the future. Until the great majority of mankind have been educated into the true democracy, until each one has grown to say in his heart, "I want the same rights and opportunities as my neighbour, and no more", until that altruistic day arrives, strong and selfish men will still somewhere continue banding together in ever broader and craftier conspiracies to snatch the pleasant richness of life from those who seem too feeble or too ignorant to resist.
These words were uttered twenty odd years ago, and I am sure they are as true now as when they were uttered. I realize, of course, that the government has a difficult time in converting Canada into an arsenal. There have been differences in specifications as between this country and the rest of the empire; frequently more difficulties and delays through the changing of specifications, and other difficulties no doubt through a desire not to set up in Canada rivalries in trade.
There have been domestic problems, the difficulty of obtaining tools and skilled mechanics. Yet the impression has spread abroad that there has been too much officiousness in this country and not enough efficiency. Of course we have these high-priced Tory dollar-a-year men like MacMillan and the rest of them who are such characters that no one will ever say a word until the minister first makes a statement, and in that way they allowed controversy to develop throughout the country, with reflections being cast on the aircraft industry. I admit, however, as the minister says, that we are a young nation. We are "in the mushroom stage", he said, but it will be necessary for us to harness all our human resources to our natural resources if we are in the years to come to be strong enough to break Germany's war machine.
Until now we have had the ministers rising in their places and making formal statements out of which one can take any meaning at all.
I was sitting on the other side of the house one day and I heard one minister say to another as he sat down, "Well done, you told them nothing."
We must educate public opinion, and in that regard we have failed badly. Before the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) made his statement in the house concerning the aircraft industry, there was a terrible feeling throughout the country. Yet when the minister gave his explanation of the aircraft situation he showed that the aircraft industry was not in such a bad plight as we thought it was. We had thought we were in a very bad spot in this particular branch of production. This could have all been cleared up if members of the house had been given the information.

War Appropriation Bill
There was a splendid address given by Mr. Carmichael over the radio to-night. He showed the production of aeroplanes in the United States and how our production was going, and he gave a satisfactory explanation to the Canadian people. That explanation, however, should have been given long, long ago, before the public mind had become unsettled. If members of the house had had any information, they could have given it out to the public, but of course they would never get any information!
People need inspiration to produce their utmost war effort. Propaganda has become one of Hitler's most important weapons in this new type of war. As J. B. Priestley pointed out in a recent radio address, Hitler tries to sap our resistance by telling us of the horrible things he is going to do to us with the aid of secret weapons and secret machines. What we should be doing is telling him and the Germans of all the horrible things we may have in store for them.
One of the most important changes that we could have in the administration would be to have a ministry of enlightenment. I realize that some of the ministers would not want that because they do not want to disturb too greatly the ordinary methods of gathering the news, but I am sure that, with the situation as it is to-day, even the newspapers cannot give accurate information any more than we can unless they are supplied with it.
The bureau of public information! If anybody ever tried to get information from that bureau, he would soon find out that it was not a bureau of information but a propaganda bureau.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: A propaganda bureau in the best sense of the word, not in the sense that the leader of the opposition takes it. I do not see why we should be afraid to call it a bureau of propaganda. Mr. Lash, the director of the bureau of public information, in its assigned task of propaganda, is doing an excellent job. But it has not gone far enough.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is he a Tory?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not know, but I
suppose so. After all, a ministry of enlightenment could serve in peace time as well as in war, and we might include in that propaganda bureau a legitimate bureau of information, the archives, the national gallery, the national film board, the Canadian Broadcasing Corporation, the historical section now working in the national defence department, and possibly the censors, although I do not think any of the newspaper men would expect to get much enlightenment out of the censors.
All of these different activities are now being carried on under a wide range of departments among which in many instances it is difficult to see any relationship. With the tremendous sums of money that are being and will be spent on our war effort, there is no reason why this information should not be gathered and given out to the public and why members of parliament and the newspapers should not have it.
Eastern Canada, and especially the central provinces, are to-day enjoying a measure of prosperity, and of course it is odd for us from the west to rise in our places in this house and say that agriculture and the primary producer were never in a worse plight than today. But wheat is a drug on the market. Farmers are unsettled in their opinion as to whether they are rendering any war service by trying to produce commodities and food products of various kinds. Mortgage companies are still collecting their interest.
With this oversupply of foodstuffs in this country we see at the same time the people of Britain on rations. It often occurs to me, why should we haggle about the price Great Britain is to pay for the commodities they buy from us? When there was overproduction in the United States during the depression they dumped their surplus products, their coffee and so forth, in the rivers, and ploughed under a great deal of their wheat. I do not see why we could not get some of this money that we seem to get so easily now for destructive purposes and use it for constructive purposes and pay our farmers for any surplus wheat or other war products that they might produce for this greatest of all causes. In the old days it was impossible to get any money, but now we can get all we want without any difficulty for destructive purposes.
"Oh," some one may say, "we have no ships." But Lord Beaverbrook said, "Go to the ends of the earth and get them." Members from British Columbia say that shipbuilding is not going on in that province to any marked degree, and members from the mari-times tell us the same thing. There are shipbuilders walking around with no work to do. I heard over the radio a few days ago that every shipbuilder in the United Kingdom had *been conscripted for war service. Why do we not do that in Canada?
"A nation cannot exist half slave and half free," said Abraham Lincoln, and there is such a thing as economic slavery. A nation cannot continue half rich and half poor.
In Saskatchewan in the pre-war depression years, with no crop in the drought areas, we went through the worst period that any province ever went through. Now, when there
War Appropriation Bill

is an opportunity to do something for those people on western Canada's plains, those plains which in more peaceful times have been called the "bread-basket of the empire" and the "granary of the empire," has any effort been made to establish industry in western Canada? No. Hundreds and hundreds of people are walking the streets looking for work. They are skilled workmen. What do they do? They come from Saskatchewan to Ontario and try to secure work in some of the munitions plants. WTiat are they told? That they are too old; "what we want are boys out of the technical schools"-boys who should be in the armed forces of the country and not taken into these places and provided with positions which should be given to these older people. Industries should have been established in Saskatchewan, and established long ago. In Saskatchewan another matter of grave importance with regard to which we have been discriminated against is the training of young tradesmen under this scheme of the labour department. The lowest vote which was allocated for this work of training young chaps was to that province. After all the hardship which our people have gone through, schools have been established only in the larger cities, although in every place throughout that province where there were sufficient applicants those schools should have been put into operation immediately. A few years ago we in the town of Humboldt had marked success with these new training schools; they did a splendid piece of work. The schools which have been sponsored by the Department of Labour would have excellent results. The young men who would be trained there would be fitted to go into the factories if they were not physically fit for the army, or, if they joined the armed forces, they would have some trade available to them upon their return to civil life when this struggle is over.
If we forsake these people on the western plains we shall be doing a grave injustice. We know that when an opportunity arose of establishing our economy on a healthier basis, certain interests sabotaged the Rowell-Sirois commission report; and that fact may yet become a stain upon our national conscience.
Citizens in every walk of life, in every province of Canada, wish to do their part in this, the testing hour of the nation. Let the government take the people of Canada into its confidence. Let them take the members of parliament into their confidence; after all they, just as much as the ministers, are representatives of the people. Let them do something to establish industry on these western plains. The people of our province will meet every financial call which may be made upon them. They

will accept every defeat that comes to us, and they will accept final victory and peace in a truly Canadian spirit. I cannot see why we should have prosperity on the banks of the Rideau and not upon the banks of the Saskatchewan.

speechtext:
I wish to make some observations in connection with the questions I asked the minister of munitions earlier in the day.
First of all, I should like to congratulate the minister upon his safe return to Canada, and particularly to congratulate the government upon his safety, because we recognize him as one of the ablest and most efficient members of the cabinet.
The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) has suggested a reason why we on this side of the chamber have not criticized the government sufficiently, namely, that so many dollar-a-year men are Tories. Therefore, if I indulge in a little criticism this evening, I hope it will be regarded as constructive, and it will be remembered that I have been invited especially to make it by the hon. member who has just spoken.
I was sorry that the minister of munitions did not lay on the table of the house this afternoon the missing pages-Nos. 5, 6, 7 and part of 8-of the MacMillan report, giving as the reason that they contain highly confidential matter about guns. The refusal to produce those pages has aroused public suspicion that the minister has some other reason for withholding them, and that he has something to conceal. I think, therefore, that it would be better for the minister himself if he did as I asked him to do and set this suspicion at rest at once.
Will the minister tell the committee if there was any subject dealt with in the deleted portion of the report in addition to the production of guns?
Were any details given as to the various types of guns being produced?
Have we developed a new secret weapon to use in this war?

Does the minister seriously think that the facts given about guns in the pages which he has deleted would help the enemy? Was there anything in those suppressed three and a half pages critical of the present method of administration or of the minister's proposed set-up for the future?

(i)	Armour plate to come from Steel Company of Canada-plant to be completed May/June 1941. May be delayed by equipment from U.S.A.

Then on page 8 under paragraph (f) the following statement is made:
The situation therefore is: Canada already has surplus aircraft production capacity but requires some planning to arrange to use it economically.
From what I have just read, it will be seen that the production of tanks is in a hopeless muddle, and yet this information is published. Surely it will help the enemy more to know that we have fallen down badly in the production of such a vital arm as tanks than to know that we are making good progress in the production of guns.
Although the attention of the house was called to the importance of tanks in June last, particularly where the component parts could be made, I am very much disappointed that after a period of eight months more progress has not been made. I should like to read from an article in the Ottawa Journal of to-day's date by Ross Munro, a correspondent living in England, as follows:
These armoured units are Britain's ace weapon to counter-attack an invading force, and every reliance is placed in the tanks. The Canadian army tank brigade and armoured division, coming overseas this year, will be a welcome addition to this fast-growing branch of the army.
War Appropriation Bill

He quotes a colonel in England as saying:
This war is going to be tanks, tanks, tanks, and I maintain the Canadians, from what we have seen of them here, will be probably the best tank fighters in the world.
From the MacMillan report it will be apparent that there will be no cruiser tanks, Mark III, available until the end of this year. May I ask the minister whether this tank brigade will be sent overseas in spite of this, and whether they must again rely on Great Britain for their equipment? On page 1124 of Hansard the minister is reported as saying:
I offer the problem of aircraft production
to anyone who cares to take it.
This would seem to indicate a degree of despair, futility and frustration. The minister indicates that the responsibility now vested in him is very onerous and he has given us a lengthy description of the principles of organization. If the situation is as the minister states-and I have no do-ubt about his sincerity, that he is anxious to do everything to further Canada's war effort-then I suggest to him that the best immediate contribution he can make is by divorcing the production of munitions from all types of politics. Why does he not do as the Ontario government did in the case of the hydroelectric system-name a commissioner and delegate full authority to him, including the selection of the required personnel to enable him to carry on efficiently and get results.
It is generally understood that Mr. MacMillan, after some months' experience as chairman of the war-time requirements board, recommended to the minister a scheme for the complete reorganization of the munitions and supply production department. May I ask the minister whether he agrees with the scheme outlined by Mr. MacMillan? If so, does he consider Mr. MacMillan sufficiently competent to be put in full charge of this scheme?
I do not happen to have the privilege of knowing Mr. MacMillan personally, but I know him very well by reputation, and, in common with the Canadian people generally,
I have great confidence in him as a high-minded patriotic citizen who is unselfishly trying to do a great public service and who, they believe, is being hampered in bis work by partisan interference.
In order to give the committee an idea of the kind of man Mr. MacMillan is, I should like to quote, from the Vancouver Daily Province of February 25 last, parts of a 
speech which he gave at a public banquet given in his honour in the city of Vancouver. I quote:
Mr. MacMillan said that in his own private organization, as in every well-run business in the country, the whole staff worked to the balance sheet. When there was anything wrong with that balance sheet the weakness was soon discovered and the correction made-in personnel or in method.
"It should be the same in our national life," said Mr. MacMillan.
"In this case the balance sheet of Canada is the war. Nothing else matters."
"If we find that our capacity for making an effective war performance-say in the supply of ships and guns and aircraft and munitions- is defective, then it should be our duty to make the needed change without delay-and we should make it with one single motive to increase the efficiency of our war effort."
"We should make it our business to see that our machinery for waging war is running smoothly, and in our effort to attain that objective we shouldn't be sidetracked by political, racial, geographical, religious or any personal considerations. AM those relatively petty things should be swept aside ruthlessly. They simply don't count."
And further on:
Every person in Canada to-day should adopt this creed-to strengthen the national war spirit and avoid destructive criticism; to develop a true war spirit, to speed war production, to follow our constitutional form of government, to maintain the strongest possible government which in turn demands a strong opposition. We are not saturated yet with the critical value of the time factor. . . .
We have been too tolerant, too tolerant of mistakes and incompetence. . . .
If the state fails in this fight or if it fails to maintain balanced intelligent government- all is lost.
I think it is fair to conclude from the quotation which I have just read that something has interfered with the operation of the department that has to do with the securing of supplies. Is it not fair also to assume that it may be on this rock that the minister and Mr. MacMillan split before the latter left for the west some weeks ago? May I again urge that the atmosphere of suspicion be cleared away. I appeal to the minister, with all the force at my command, to make a frank statement himself and ask Mr. MacMillan to do the same, covering all the questions asked by me on Monday last, and thus relieve the public anxiety and suspicion that something is being hidden and that there exists a sharp conflict of opinion as to policy and administration between Mr. MacMillan and the minister.
I wish now to quote from an editorial in what we all have regarded as a Liberal newspaper. the Globe and Mail of March 4, 1941.

When Canada and all parts of the British empire are giving their blood and treasure, they have a right to demand that there shall be no delay in the production of guns, aeroplanes and other munitions of war with which to protect them and upon the speedy supply of which our very existence depends. And we are not going to take any form of dictatorship, no matter who the minister is.
While I am on my feet I should like to make one or two observations along the lines of those I made at the last session. I am greatly concerned with the manner in which the department sees fit to spend money as capital expenditure for new buildings, when so many first-class buildings are available. To a large degree, in many of the large centres buildings are under construction, with steel work completed, which could be taken over by the department, or by those who are accepting contracts, or who are accepting moneys for working capital in connection with carrying out the contracts they have in hand.
I would place on record facts respecting three premises of real magnitude in an area within one or two miles of the John Inglis plant at Toronto, a plant in which large sums are being spent by way of capital expenditure. When I have recorded these facts I shall resume my seat.
First, I should like to mention a building which will soon be completed and which is owned by the Dominion of Canada. I refer to the post office building at the corner of Fleet and Yonge streets in the city of Toronto. Acres of floor space are available in that building. The building is completed. It is not yet occupied. At this point let me digress for a moment. If buildings of this kind were taken over by the Department of Munitions and Supply and put into production

War Appropriation Bill
for war purposes, our people would be seized with the idea more and more that we are at war. They would tend to give more thought and more energy and would subscribe to more war savings certificates-and I ask the Minister of Finance to take note-if the department would take over buildings of the kind I have mentioned.
The second building I have in mind is at the corner of King and Bay streets. This is a large bank building, the steel construction now reaching the ninth and tenth floors. Several acres of floor space are available. Foundations are laid down to bedrock thirty-five feet below the ground. Work to complete that building has been stopped. Perhaps it is not the exact type which would be required for the work being done so extensively by the John Inglis plant. But we do know that new buildings not nearly as well constructed as the one I have mentioned are being built, from the ground up, and that there is delay in having them built. Here is a building the main structure of which is completed. The ministry should take charge of it, brick it in and have a war industry right at the corner of King and Bay streets in the heart of Toronto. Would the people in that area not be seized with the idea that there is a war on? Would they not give more and more attention to the war effort?
The third building I have in mind is one operated under a lease by the National Stone company on Logan avenue, in Toronto. It is a building 300 feet by 300 feet, and) is equipped with a total of eight cranes, some of which will lift loads of fifty tons. The siding is constructed, and would lend itself admirably to some of those contractors who are using some of the working capital we are voting, to build new structures. They need not spend that money for new structures when a structure of the kind I am describing is available, and lends itself admirably to the job of completing war contracts, and to speeding up and getting on with war work.
What obtains with regard to those three large structures I have mentioned, one of which is controlled by the government, one by a banking institution and the third by an estate, obtains elsewhere in the same city. I have mentioned just those three. I have in mind, of course, the non-practicability, as it were, of doing jobs of work on a smaller scale, and having different operations separated one from another. But I bring to the attention of the department, many, many, many contracts which could be completed in buildings already available.

speechtext:
The discussions so far on this resolution which was before the house and which is now before the committee have been largely with regard to expenditures having to do with munitions and supply. I think it was February 25 when the discussions began. Since that time I have been waiting for an opportunity to make a few remarks with regard to the particular part of the war effort charged up to and coming under the Department of National War Sendees. I desire to make -these remarks at -this time partly because of certain information which is available now and which neither the house nor the public know of at the moment and partly because of certain criticisms which were made prior to the meeting of the house with regard to the reasons for the registration, the method by which it was carried out, and the results obtained.
It will be recalled that when the Department of National War Services was set up, there was assigned to it the task of making a registration of the human resources of Canada and, in due course, of making a survey with regard to the material resources. The department was asked also to take charge of the bureau of information, which has been referred to from time to time during the debate. We were asked to bring about, if possible, the coordination of the efforts of those who were engaged in collecting from the people of Canada funds with which to carry on volun-taiy services.

The task given to the department in connection with the registration had for its objective two different results. The first was to obtain men for the training camps. The initial desire of the Department of National Defence was that these training camps should be operated for thirty days and that something between 25,000 and 30,000 men should be obtained for six weeks in order to fill the camps. Before a call could be sent forth to the young men required for these camps, it was necessary to have a registration in order to know where they were. In addition to that, it was thought wise to -make a registration of all persons from sixteen years upwards in order that we might know something of the capabilities -of the general population of Canada and also have a better check upon that population. I think some of the remarks made in the House of Commons at the time, most of them by hon. members of the opposition, which I intend to quote in a few moments, indicate as clearly as anything else the feeling with regard to the registration itself.
Before going on to deal with the registration, I should like to add my protest to the protests made by other members of the government, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I do not protest because criticism of the government has been offered or because there has been criticism of this particular department or of the registration; I protest simply to draw attention to the nature of the criticism which has been offered by certain sections of the press across Canada. I have no objection at any time to criticism; as a matter of fact I invite it, provided it is based upon facts and not upon statements which are not facts. I admit that criticism, particularly in war time, is helpful. It has been said that ministers in the government have too much to do, and yet many times those who say that have been adding more to the tasks of these ministers than any other group or organization in the Dominion of Canada. This criticism has appeared in newspapers across Canada with large circulations. They -have published what are not the facts and have made criticism which was not based upon things being done in the different departments of the government.
When criticism of that kind is offered it requires more effort and uses up more nervous strain and delays the activities of the particular department more than anything else being done, either inside or outside the dominion. When once wrong information is given -to the people of Canada by the press of the country, it is necessary for the department and the minister involved to clear up such criticism before the effort being put forth by the department can be carried on to

War Appropriation Bill
a successful conclusion. There has been much criticism of members of the government as to why this or that has not been done, as to why there has been delay in doing this or that.
Those who were criticized should be and, I think, are expected to make answers to the criticisms, and probably to criticize those who made the criticisms. My criticism of the press, more particularly a certain section of the press, would be this, that there is no organized group in the dominion that has done more since the fall of 1939 to delay the war effort of this country than certain sections of the press in Canada. That effort started even before war was declared, and it has been carried on since.
I agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) when he says it is a mistake politically to get into a controversy with the press because experience has shown that they always have the last word and that if you start an argument with them you are starting something which you cannot end. Nevertheless I believe at times it is necessary that the facts with regard to criticisms of that kind should be stated and that someone should say what he considers to be the effect of that kind of criticism upon the war effort.
In times of war none of us is so much concerned about the political effect of his remarks as he is in times of peace, and if it is necessary to dispute the opinions and expressions given through the press in war time, we must do so despite the political effects it may have.
Some criticisms have been made with regard to the method by which the registration of man-power or the human resources of Canada was carried out. In order to clear up any misunderstanding there may be with regard to the registration itself, either as to the reasons for it, or as to the methods by which it was done, or as to the results obtained, I wish to give a review of what took place in that connection.

Anything I have to say with regard to the question just raised I shall say as I go along.
The government of Great Britain conducted a national registration either immediately after or immediately prior to the outbreak of war. Australia, New Zealand, south Africa, and I think most other parts of the empire did the same thing immediately after the outbreak of war. It was suggested in this country by some-I do not think by any members of the opposition-that since we were going to have a census taken in 1941, a registration in Canada perhaps was not as necessary as it otherwise might have been last year. But there is a difference between a national registration and a census. In a census you secure information, and that is the end of your contact with the individual from whom you secure the information. But a national registration is a continuing process in that it involves each individual registered carrying a national registration certificate, and records of changes of address, changes of marital status and death being continually kept.
Following the collapse of France, there was an insistent demand both within and without parliament that there should be a national registration in Canada. I have taken the trouble to go through Hansard and obtain from it the requests by different members that a national registration be made. There are quite a number of them, making up some seven pages of extracts of a few sentences from the speeches of different members. I shall read only one or two to indicate that these requests came from different parts of the house. The hon. member for St. Paul? (Mr. Ross) said, speaking in the house on tin 24th of May last:
In my view we should have a national regis. tration of every man and woman in Canada; if we do not, I wonder how we are going to find out about subversive influences?
The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), speaking in the house on May 27 last, said:
The general feeling among the people to whom I spoke is that one way of overcoming this trouble is to have a national registration of the men and women of the country with a view to having a list of those available for war work.
Then the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser), who in commenting the other day upon the salvage campaign had the kindly thought to add to his remarks with

War Appropriation Bill

regard to it that we might term the Ministry of National War Services the Ministry of Garbage, had this to say:
The hon. member for Waterloo South suggested that we have national registration. With that I wholly agree, and I do not mean that we should have it in 1941.
I think that is sufficient to indicate that there was a request for national registration from the opposition side of the house; I could cite remarks made by members in each of the other groups as well as by members on this side to indicate that the request was made generally throughout the house, and finally it was agreed that a national registration should be made.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition called my attention to the fact that an appeal was made to the members. That appeal was made first by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), that all the members of the house should be asked to assist in the making of this registration, and that appeal was answered from this side of the house with consent to do so. As members of the house know, to that end each member was asked to take charge of the organization in his own constituency, and the voluntary effort that was put forth as a result of the efforts of the members of this house was something of which every member can well be proud.
The only further reference I have to make to the remark of the hon. member for Peterborough West is this, that the second effort we have made to enlist the support of all members of the house was when we appealed to them to assist National War Services in connection with its salvage campaign, and there again, so far as I know, the greater part of the members are participating in this voluntary effort in the same spirit as that in which they undertook to help in the work of national registration.
But I would say this, that it is not particularly helpful or encouraging to the minister who appeals to members to do that kind of thing when we have the type of criticism that we have had from one or two within the house with regard to that particular campaign.

Next, a committee representative of all departments of the government which would be concerned with the information to be procured from the national registration was set up in June last, under the chairmanship of Doctor R. H. Coats, dominion statistician. This committee prepared a questionnaire which was subsequently submitted to the Canadian people. Only one addition thereto was suggested by the government, and that was question 17 which was added to those on the questionnaire and which asked registrants if there was any special training they would like to receive in connection with industry.
The government decided, as a matter of policy, that the national registration should be conducted under the direction of a new Department of National War Services, and the registration was conducted under my direction as minister and under the deputy ministers who were appointed for that department.
Then the committee, under the chairmanship of Doctor Coats, recommended that the actual registration should be done on an electoral division basis, as nearly as possible in the manner of an enumeration for a dominion election, and through the instrumentality of the chief electoral officer and his staff. This recommendation was accepted; the chief electoral officer was appointed chief registrar, and the actual registration was carried out under his direction.
General supervision of the registration was carried on by the associate deputy minister of the department, that is, Mr. Justice Davis.
The said committee, under Doctor Coats, further recommended that, when the registration was completed, the information secured thereby should be compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics. This recommendation was likewise accepted by the government.
I wish at this point to explain that there have been no staffs in the Department of National War Services associated with the compilation and recording of these statistics. Those staffs have been entirely in the bureau of statistics in the Department of Trade and Commerce. The staffs have been supplied by moneys secured under the vote which we are now discussing in the house, as a result of an appeal made to the government by the minister in charge of war services.
It was necessary to provide a new building for the housing of the equipment and staff necessary to do the compiling of this information. This building was completed on

War Appropriation Bill
or about the 30th of September, 1940. This, I would like to comment, was not bad, considering the fact the department was not established until the month of July. The registration was under way, and the building was completed in time for the information to be taken to that building and the staff to be employed in it.
The dominion bureau of statistics completed moving into the building and the setting up of all necessary machinery about the middle of October; the hundreds of tons of registration cards which accumulated between this date and the completion of national registration were taken over by the dominion bureau of statistics, and the actual work of compilation was started.
The first job which confronted the dominion bureau of statistics was as follows: It was the duty of the deputy registrars in the various polls to copy the cards of the single men, 19 to 45, so that copies could be used for military purposes. When the cards came in, it was found that some constituencies had made copies but sent them here. In other constituencies no copies had been made. The bureau of statistics had to get busy at once to straighten this out and furnish the divisional registrars with missing cards.
The next job undertaken was the compilation of the material with respect to Doukhobors and Japanese. This latter was urgently required for consideration by a committee dealing with the Japanese problem on the Pacific coast.
Prior to the national registration, consideration had to be given to the problem of priority in the matter of compilation of accumulated material, and a decision had to be reached as to whether or not the first job would be to get the statistical picture of the human resources of Canada, namely, the number of males and females of different ages, classified into provinces, according to occupations, nationality, condition of health, et cetera.
This information could be used only for the purpose of deciding broad matters of governmental policy with respect to the utilization of man-power in Canada. You would know from these statistical studies, for instance, how many plumbers there were in Canada, what provinces they were in, information with respect to their experience, age, nationality, et cetera, but you would not know who the actual plumbers were or where they were.
A different method of compilation was necessary in order to procure the last mentioned information. That is, it was thought that it was more important for the time being that we get statistical information which would show the name of the individual, where the 14873-84}
individual was living, and what that individual was able to do, than it was to get the broad statistical picture first in order to formulate government policies upon it.
Prior to the outbreak of war, a committee, representative of several departments of government, had been formed to prepare a list of what might be termed "reserved, preferred or specialized occupations". It was not the intention that they should be reserved in the sense that these persons would not be available for war service, but it was intended that they should be persons who were prepared for work in some industry which would be essential to the carrying on of the war. This means a list of occupations which would be directly or indirectly connected with industries necessary to war and in respect of which consideration would have to be given to the wisdom of withdrawing persons therefrom to permit them to enter the armed forces.
This list, as enlarged by the dominion bureau of statistics, contained approximately 1,250 occupations. That is, the bureau of statistics divided these different industries which might be considered essential or preferred into 1,250 different groups. It should be pointed out that this list was prepared on an occupational basis and not on the basis of industries. For instance, a man might be working in an occupation in a war-time industry, which occupation itself would not be a specialized or trained occupation, and his withdrawal from such industry would not prevent or interfere with the proper functioning of the industry. The case of the common labourer would be an instance in point.
It was decided on the advice of a committee, headed by Doctor Coats, that the first job to do was to get out a list of persons engaged in these "specialized, reserved or preferred occupations", and that the procuring of the general statistical picture should await the preparation of this list.
As soon as the national registration cards in the possession of the dominion statistician were in a position to be used, they were gone through. Incidentally, the dominion statistician received about eight million cards as a result of the national registration. From these eight million cards there were extracted approximately 1,800,000 cards of males and females who belonged to these "specialized or reserved occupations".
This group was then broken down into three categories, which were made up from the answers to these three questions: No. 14, occupation or craft; (a) present occupation (b) what is your regular occupation? (c) what other work can you do well? Through those three questions there were selected the persons that constituted these different groups,
War Appropriation Bill

although they did not take in all the persons who answered those questions. Some of the answers did not show them to belong to these specialized groups.
As I have said, this group was broken down into three categories or three lots as follows:
(a)	A list of persons trained in these specialized or reserved occupations and presently engaged therein.
(b)	A list of persons whose regular occupation was a specialized or reserved occupation but who were not at the time of registration working in their regular occupations. They might be temporarily engaged) in some other reserved occupation but, at all events, not in their regular occupation.
(c)	A list of persons who had training in a specialized or reserved occupation but were not presently engaged in such occupation, or whose regular occupation was not the occupation in which they had special training.
These lists-three in number, as above indicated-also show persons with training in any of these reserved occupations who were unemployed. I may say that I have before me that list with regard to the province of Ontario, and the figures on that list illustrate very well the situation existing in that province. Very shortly, figures will be ready for all the provinces of Canada upon this basis. Just to illustrate the nature of the information which is available with regard to these
1,800,000	persons, may I call attention to this: In Ontario there are about 1,300,000 males of the ages that we are concerned with here in that province among whom these cards have been selected, and in dealing with those specialized classes to which I have referred, we find that 444,496 persons are at present engaged in the industry for which they are best qualified. There are 170,856 in the second group I spoke of; that is, they are not engaged in the industry for which they consider themselves best qualified, although they may be engaged in some other war industry. Then there are 289,948 who are engaged at something else, but who stated that they had had experience in doing work in some of those activities that are necessary to the carrying on of the war.
Turning over a number of pages, and coming to a group that might be of interest, let us look at miners and see how the group that have had experience or are properly qualified to be miners are divided up in Ontario. There are 15,136 persons specially qualified to work in mines and who are working in manes; 5,29.3 qualified to work in mines are not working in mines but are working at some other industry which might be important in connection with the war, for which they do not

consider themselves quite as well qualified; 3,998 persons in Ontario have had experience in working in mines but are not working in mines now.
That will give some idea of the nature of the information available in connection with all these different 1,250 occupations spoken of in connection with these services.
Coming down to electrical apparatus, an employment in connection with which there is great importance as related to the war effort, we find that 6,909 persons in Ontario are working at part of the job for which they are best qualified; 2,664 are working somewhere but not where they think they are best qualified; 5,950 have qualifications to work in that industry but are not working in it. They are engaged, probably, in some other effort that may be made in connection with the war, but not in that one.
Then, coming to electrical repair men and service men, we find there are 1,950 men working where they think they are best equipped to work; 1,799 in the second class; and 4,242 in the third class. The third class, which is the one from which persons could be drawn and moved into an industry that they feel they can do a better job in than they are doing now, is more than twice as great as the number regularly working in that particular employment.
That is sufficient to indicate the nature of the information which is available now with regard to Ontario and which will be available very shortly with regard to all the provinces.
To give a little more detail as to what can be obtained as a result of that class of information being registered, may I say the result is that we have a list of all persons at present engaged in these reserved occupations, those engaged in other occupations but capable by training of being used in these reserved occupations, and those unemployed, capable of employment in these reserved occupations- that is, unemployed in these particular occupations.
To emphasize the vastness of the job which was required to be done, I am told that there are twelve miles of these names-that the sheets, with the names on them, could be piled from the floor up to the ceiling of any of the rooms where these documents are stored. I am told that you can go into the statistical department to-day where the lists are completely made up, as they are in Ontario, and, by tests up to date, inside two or three minutes a clerk can get you the name of any person who is on the list. He will get you information to show the address of that person, what he is working at, what he thinks he is capable of working at and not working

War Appropriation Bill
at. In other words, these lists are available. They have been made available to all the departments of government and are being used by the different departments.
These lists are now available for the industries of Canada and are being used by some of them. Let me give a concrete example to show how they can be used in a direct way. A manufacturing firm desire to know where they can find a list of persons with that particular type of training. For instance, they may want to know where they can locate tool makers. From these lists the dominion bureau of statistics can furnish to the industry the names, addresses, age, nationality, birthplace, years of experience, et cetera, and whether or not now employed, of all tool makers in Canada or in a given province or district in Canada. This applies to each of the 1,250 specialized or reserved occupations.
That last remark will apply within the next few days, when the statistical information is completed, to all the provinces. At the present time it covers a very considerable part of Canada and is entirely completed for Ontario.
In this way any industry seeking men to be engaged can be given the names, addresses and locations of such individuals and can be advised whether or not they are working in that trade or in any other trade, and whether they are employed or unemployed. This was a tremendous job and was completed at the end of January. As soon as it was completed, steps were taken to procure the same type of information in connection with agriculture, and these agricultural lists will be available very shortly for the provinces of Canada.
On completion of this work, the dominion statistician then turned attention to the preparation of the statistical tables necessary for the use of the government and the departments of government-that is, for the formulation of general policy. The first series of statistical tables being prepared gives statistical information with respect to the lists of specialized or reserved occupations which I have mentioned. It gives us a statistical picture of the numbers at present employed in these specialized or reserved occupations, those whose regular occupation is a specialized or reserved occupation, and those who have had training in such specialized or reserved occupation.
These are broken down by sex, age groups and occupational status. Then a statistical study is being made of the registration as a whole-that is, a statistical study of the entire 8,000,000 cards. I have here certain information, again with regard to Ontario, which I am not going to go over except to
say that if the house would permit me to do so I should like to have this short table put on Hansard, because it gives simply the total population of Ontario over sixteen years of age, dividing it into age groups, into males and females.

That is the nature of the information which is being made up with regard to the whole population, the eight million people in Canada. This statistical picture will show the number of males and females, with emphasis on the following break-down: age, conjugal condition, birthplace, birthplace of parents, year of immigration if an immigrant, year of naturalization, racial origin, official languages spoken, other languages than English and French spoken, educational status, condition of health, disabilities, pension status, occupational and employment status, weeks since last employment if unemployed, weeks worked in twelve months prior to August 1, 1940, farm back-

ground, experience with horses, tractors and machinery, experience in milking and other farm work.
This will be followed by an industrial classification together with statistics as to numbers of dependents, family occupations, complete details as to occupations et cetera. These statistics for the province of Ontario I intend to file. I do not think I have a copy here to-night, but I will file it to-morrow.
The same information for all the other provinces of Canada will be completed shortly and will be duly filed.
Arrangements have been made with the various departments of the government that any department wishing to procure information with respect to name, address and location of persons, whether employed or unemployed, with any particular type of training will requisition this information from the dominion bureau of statistics, and lists will be immediately furnished.
It is interesting to note that tremendous use is being made of this national registration by the police forces of Canada. I remember one lion, member, I think it was the hon. member for Waterloo South, who made reference to that in the house when advocating that this registration should be made, that these lists would be most useful, and hon. members will recall that on the first day after the registration was made one of the German prisoners who had escaped from the camp was captured going across a bridge, because he did not have a registration card. In other words, that information is most valuable, as was stated by hon. members and others at the time. A staff of clerks is engaged continuously in getting out information for the police authorities.
It was decided to procure lists of all citizens in Canada of the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark, Norway, Poland, Czechoslovakia, showing the names, addresses, marital relationship, ages, et cetera. This information was to be used for the military purposes of these governments. That is, these governments, as hon. members know, are practically all being conducted now somewhere outside their own countries, and when they wish to get the names of their nationals living in this country they are able to do so and communicate with those nationals if they so desire.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I said at the beginning of my remarks, when I think the hon. member

was not in his seat, that there is a difference between a census and these statistics. The census is not my responsibility, and I prefer that the minister who is responsible should make his own statement in regard to it.
This information has already been put to use 'by the governments of Belgium, Poland and Holland.
The national registration was conducted on a constituency basis. When the registration cards came in, they were kept separate by constituencies and polling subdivisions. We are now engaged in rearranging these cards on an alphabetical basis, using the system known as the "soundex" system, which has been adopted from that used by the census bureau of the United States. As soon as this work is completed, if the name of a given individual is handed to the dominion statistician he can at once get out the card of such individual, thus permitting a constant check on the entire population of Canada.
I had the intention of dealing to-night also with a reference to the information bureau, but I see that it is now two minutes to eleven, and I do not think I shall undertake to make that statement to-night. I shall leave it for another occasion, either while we are discussing this resolution in committee or when we are discussing the individual estimate. But I wish, on behalf of the staff of the statistical branch, and the staff that was got together to assist tthe chief electoral officer, and on behalf of every member of the staff of the Department of National War Services, to thank each and every hon. member for the willing and effective cooperation which they gave to make a registration of this kind possible in the very short time in which it was done. I do not think the credit for it is due to the department or the minister or the deputy minister, or to any individual anywhere. It is due, first, to those who advocated the matter in this house and consented to its being done. In the second place it is due to the hon. members who cooperated in seeing that we got the greatest degree possible of cooperation in setting up voluntary organizations to help in the work, and also to the whole-hearted way in which all the people from one end of Canada to the other went into these registration booths in such numbers that in some places we had to get the police to regulate the passing of the people into the booths. In other words, the job was not to get them there but to handle them in the numbers in which they came, and the only reason why that was not an impossible job was that every booth was manned-or "womaned," if I may so express it-by staffs capable of doing this registration
